papers.conclusion: SAEs are a valuable tool for understanding InceptionV1 and convolutional neural networks, extending their promise beyond language models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs learn new interpretable features that were not visible when examining individual neurons.
SAEs discover additional curve detector features that fill gaps in the known family of curve detectors.
SAEs can split polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic constituent features.
papers.limitation: This paper is a very early report and does not defend the results in a systematic way.
future_direction: Investigate branch specialization and cross-branch superposition in InceptionV1 using SAEs.
papers.abstract: Recent work on sparse autoencoders (SAEs) has shown promise in extracting interpretable features from neural networks and addressing challenges with polysemantic neurons caused by superposition. In this paper, we apply SAEs to the early vision layers of InceptionV1, a well-studied convolutional neural network, with a focus on curve detectors. Our results demonstrate that SAEs can uncover new interpretable features not apparent from examining individual neurons, including additional curve detectors that fill in previous gaps. We also find that SAEs can decompose some polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic constituent features. These findings suggest SAEs are a valuable tool for understanding InceptionV1, and convolutional neural networks more generally.

papers.title: SOSAE: Self-Organizing Sparse AutoEncoder
papers.research_question: How can the dimensionality of an autoencoder's feature space be dynamically and optimally adapted without extensive hyperparameter tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SOSAE, a self-organizing sparse autoencoder that uses a novel push regularization to dynamically optimize the size of feature representations during training, achieving efficient compression and feature extraction.
papers.conclusion: SOSAE effectively optimizes feature representation size via push regularization, significantly reducing computational and memory costs while maintaining model performance across various image datasets.
papers.key_findings:
SOSAE compresses input into significantly smaller feature lengths (3.1 to 4.3 times more compression) than baseline autoencoders while maintaining or improving classification accuracy.
SOSAE reduces FLOPs usage by 23.3% to 32% and memory usage significantly compared to baselines, due to structured sparsity and truncation of non-active neurons.
The feature vectors generated by SOSAE are robust to truncation; removing trailing dimensions does not cause information loss, unlike other sparse autoencoder variants.
SOSAE achieves optimal hidden layer dimensionality with up to 130 times fewer FLOPs than grid search and 34 times fewer than random search for hyperparameter tuning.
SOSAE demonstrates better denoising performance and robustness against zero-masking and Gaussian noise compared to Denoising Autoencoders, while using shorter feature representations.
papers.abstract: The process of tuning the size of the hidden layers for autoencoders has the benefit of providing optimally compressed representations for the input data. However, such hyper-parameter tuning process would take a lot of computation and time effort with grid search as the default option. In this paper, we introduce the Self-Organization Regularization for Autoencoders that dynamically adapts the dimensionality of the feature space to the optimal size. Inspired by physics concepts, Self-Organizing Sparse AutoEncoder (SOSAE) induces sparsity in feature space in a structured way that permits the truncation of the non-active part of the feature vector without any loss of information. This is done by penalizing the autoencoder based on the magnitude and the positional index of the feature vector dimensions, which during training constricts the feature space in both terms. Extensive experiments on various datasets show that our SOSAE can tune the feature space dimensionality up to 130 times lesser Floating-point Operations (FLOPs) than other baselines while maintaining the same quality of tuning and performance.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Reveal Temporal Difference Learning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models implement temporal difference learning to solve reinforcement learning problems in-context, despite being trained only for next-token prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models implement temporal difference learning for in-context reinforcement learning, and sparse autoencoders can reveal and causally manipulate these representations.
papers.conclusion: The work shows that large language models implement temporal difference learning for in-context reinforcement learning, and sparse autoencoders provide a methodology for studying and manipulating these mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Llama 3 70B can solve simple reinforcement learning problems in-context and its behavior is best described by a Q-learning model.
Sparse autoencoders trained on the residual stream reveal features that correlate with temporal difference errors and Q-values.
Intervening on these temporal difference features (lesioning or clamping) impairs performance and reduces correlations, demonstrating their causal involvement.
In a grid world task, Llama uses temporal difference-like features to predict the actions of a Q-learning agent.
In a graph learning task, Llama learns global graph structure similarly to the successor representation, and temporal difference features support this learning.
papers.limitation:
The sparse autoencoders are task-specific and not suitable for identifying reinforcement learning variables for arbitrary tasks.
A circuit-level understanding of how these representations come about remains unclear.
The alignment between the model's behavior and the Q-learning agent is not perfect.
future_direction: Build more generic sparse autoencoders for arbitrary tasks.
Replicate findings with different large language models.
Achieve a circuit-level understanding of how temporal difference representations are computed.
Extend the Q-learning model to account for repetition tendencies.
papers.abstract: In-context learning, the ability to adapt based on a few examples in the input prompt, is a ubiquitous feature of large language models (LLMs). However, as LLMs' in-context learning abilities continue to improve, understanding this phenomenon mechanistically becomes increasingly important. In particular, it is not well-understood how LLMs learn to solve specific classes of problems, such as reinforcement learning (RL) problems, in-context. Through three different tasks, we first show that Llama $3$ $70$B can solve simple RL problems in-context. We then analyze the residual stream of Llama using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and find representations that closely match temporal difference (TD) errors. Notably, these representations emerge despite the model only being trained to predict the next token. We verify that these representations are indeed causally involved in the computation of TD errors and $Q$-values by performing carefully designed interventions on them. Taken together, our work establishes a methodology for studying and manipulating in-context learning with SAEs, paving the way for a more mechanistic understanding.

papers.title: Are Sparse Autoencoders Useful? A Case Study in Sparse Probing
papers.research_question: Do sparse autoencoders (SAEs) improve performance on LLM activation probing tasks in challenging regimes such as data scarcity, class imbalance, label noise, and covariate shift?
papers.core_contribution: SAE probes do not consistently outperform baseline probing methods across various challenging regimes, and baseline methods can achieve similar interpretability insights.
papers.conclusion: Current SAEs do not offer a consistent advantage for probing tasks, highlighting the need for rigorous evaluation of interpretability methods with strong baselines.
papers.key_findings:
SAE probes underperform baseline logistic regression on average across datasets in standard conditions.
SAE probes do not provide a consistent advantage in data scarcity, class imbalance, label noise, and covariate shift regimes.
Baseline methods can provide similar interpretability insights as SAE probes, such as detecting dataset issues.
Pruning SAE latents based on autointerp descriptions can slightly improve out-of-distribution generalization but not enough to match the performance drop.
SAE latents sometimes fail to generalize out-of-distribution, e.g., a latent for 'living room' only fires on English phrases.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to probing tasks and may not generalize to other tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for interpreting concepts represented in large language model (LLM) activations. However, there is a lack of evidence regarding the validity of their interpretations due to the lack of a ground truth for the concepts used by an LLM, and a growing number of works have presented problems with current SAEs. One alternative source of evidence would be demonstrating that SAEs improve performance on downstream tasks beyond existing baselines. We test this by applying SAEs to the real-world task of LLM activation probing in four regimes: data scarcity, class imbalance, label noise, and covariate shift. Due to the difficulty of detecting concepts in these challenging settings, we hypothesize that SAEs' basis of interpretable, concept-level latents should provide a useful inductive bias. However, although SAEs occasionally perform better than baselines on individual datasets, we are unable to design ensemble methods combining SAEs with baselines that consistently outperform ensemble methods solely using baselines. Additionally, although SAEs initially appear promising for identifying spurious correlations, detecting poor dataset quality, and training multi-token probes, we are able to achieve similar results with simple non-SAE baselines as well. Though we cannot discount SAEs' utility on other tasks, our findings highlight the shortcomings of current SAEs and the need to rigorously evaluate interpretability methods on downstream tasks with strong baselines.

papers.title: SAEBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Sparse Autoencoders in Language Model Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate dictionary learning (sparse autoencoders) for language model interpretability beyond unsupervised proxy metrics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAEBench, a comprehensive benchmark with eight metrics to evaluate sparse autoencoders for language model interpretability, and provides an open-source suite of over 200 SAEs for systematic comparison.
papers.conclusion: SAEBench provides a standardized framework for evaluating SAEs, revealing that proxy metrics are insufficient and that different architectures excel at different aspects of interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Gains on proxy metrics (sparsity-fidelity) do not reliably translate to better practical performance.
Matryoshka SAEs perform well on feature disentanglement metrics despite underperforming on proxy metrics.
Scaling SAE width has mixed effects: some metrics improve, but feature disentanglement metrics often degrade except for Matryoshka SAEs.
No single sparsity level is optimal for all tasks; moderate sparsity (L0 50-150) offers a reasonable compromise.
ReLU SAEs are outperformed by newer architectures on most metrics.
papers.limitation: The metrics were designed for evaluating SAEs on the same underlying model, not for comparing SAEs across fundamentally different models such as fully trained versus randomly initialized.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular technique for interpreting language model activations, and there is extensive recent work on improving SAE effectiveness. However, most prior work evaluates progress using unsupervised proxy metrics with unclear practical relevance. We introduce SAEBench, a comprehensive evaluation suite that measures SAE performance across eight diverse metrics, spanning interpretability, feature disentanglement and practical applications like unlearning. To enable systematic comparison, we open-source a suite of over 200 SAEs across eight recently proposed SAE architectures and training algorithms. Our evaluation reveals that gains on proxy metrics do not reliably translate to better practical performance. For instance, while Matryoshka SAEs slightly underperform on existing proxy metrics, they substantially outperform other architectures on feature disentanglement metrics; moreover, this advantage grows with SAE scale. By providing a standardized framework for measuring progress in SAE development, SAEBench enables researchers to study scaling trends and make nuanced comparisons between different SAE architectures and training methodologies. Our interactive interface enables researchers to flexibly visualize relationships between metrics across hundreds of open-source SAEs at: www.neuronpedia.org/sae-bench

papers.title: Kronecker Factorization Improves Efficiency and Interpretability of Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the computational efficiency and interpretability of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for language model interpretation? Specifically, can a Kronecker-factorized encoder with a novel activation function reduce costs while maintaining reconstruction quality and yielding more interpretable features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces KronSAE, a Kronecker-factorized sparse autoencoder with the mAND activation function, which reduces encoder computational cost and parameters while maintaining reconstruction fidelity and improving feature interpretability by reducing absorption.
papers.conclusion: KronSAE provides an efficient and interpretable alternative to standard sparse autoencoders, especially in resource-constrained settings, by synergizing Kronecker factorization and logical AND-style interactions to improve feature disentanglement.
papers.key_findings:
KronSAE achieves reconstruction quality comparable to baseline SAEs (TopK, Matryoshka, Switch) under iso-FLOPs constraints while using fewer parameters.
The architecture reduces feature absorption and yields more interpretable (monosemantic) latents, as measured by lower absorption scores and higher automated interpretability scores.
The mAND activation function and head-wise Cartesian decomposition are key design choices that enforce compositional structure and AND-like interactions, improving disentanglement.
KronSAE's pre-latents are often polysemantic, while post-latents are more specific, with retrieval mechanisms resembling logical AND operations.
The method introduces a trade-off between interpretability, efficiency, and reconstruction performance, controllable via hyperparameters (m, n, h).
papers.limitation: KronSAE introduces a trade-off between interpretability, efficiency, and reconstruction performance.
future_direction: Further exploration of the trade-offs and applications of KronSAE.
Developing more sophisticated techniques to identify the fine-grained structure of interactions between pre-latents.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have demonstrated significant promise in interpreting the hidden states of language models by decomposing them into interpretable latent directions. However, training and interpreting SAEs at scale remains challenging, especially when large dictionary sizes are used. While decoders can leverage sparse-aware kernels for efficiency, encoders still require computationally intensive linear operations with large output dimensions. To address this, we propose KronSAE, a novel architecture that factorizes the latent representation via Kronecker product decomposition, drastically reducing memory and computational overhead. Furthermore, we introduce mAND, a differentiable activation function approximating the binary AND operation, which improves interpretability and performance in our factorized framework.

papers.title: Understanding sparse autoencoder scaling in the presence of feature manifolds
papers.research_question: How do feature manifolds influence the scaling behavior of sparse autoencoders, and can they cause pathological scaling where SAEs allocate too many latents to common manifolds at the expense of discovering rarer features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper adapts a capacity-allocation model to sparse autoencoders, revealing that feature manifolds can lead to pathological scaling where SAEs allocate excessive latents to common manifolds, potentially hindering feature discovery.
papers.conclusion: The work frames the problem of SAE scaling and identifies conditions for pathological scaling, but it remains uncertain whether real SAEs are in this regime due to unknown feature geometry and frequency distributions.
papers.key_findings:
The model recovers distinct scaling regimes for SAEs: one where feature discovery keeps pace with latent count, and another where latents accumulate on common feature manifolds.
When the per-feature loss scaling exponent β is less than the feature frequency exponent α, SAEs enter a pathological regime where they learn far fewer features than the number of latents.
Experiments on synthetic manifolds show that the loss scaling curve depends on manifold geometry; some manifolds allow gradual loss reduction with more latents, while others saturate quickly.
Analysis of real SAEs (Gemma Scope and Inception-v1) shows some latents with high cosine similarity, but evidence for pathological tiling is inconclusive.
The presence of radial variation in feature manifolds may cause SAEs to learn basis-like solutions rather than tiling, suggesting pathological scaling might not occur in practice.
papers.limitation:
The assumptions of feature-specific latents, decoder respect for subspaces, and orthogonal feature subspaces may not hold in practice (e.g., due to feature absorption and non-orthogonality).
The model assumes power-law distributions for feature frequencies and loss scaling, which may not accurately reflect real data.
The question of whether SAEs are in the pathological regime is not resolved due to uncertainty about real feature geometries and frequencies.
future_direction: Estimating the feature frequency exponent α and loss scaling exponent β for real SAEs.
Studying the geometry of real feature manifolds to better understand SAE scaling behavior.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) model the activations of a neural network as linear combinations of sparsely occurring directions of variation (latents). The ability of SAEs to reconstruct activations follows scaling laws w.r.t. the number of latents. In this work, we adapt a capacity-allocation model from the neural scaling literature (Brill, 2024) to understand SAE scaling, and in particular, to understand how "feature manifolds" (multi-dimensional features) influence scaling behavior. Consistent with prior work, the model recovers distinct scaling regimes. Notably, in one regime, feature manifolds have the pathological effect of causing SAEs to learn far fewer features in data than there are latents in the SAE. We provide some preliminary discussion on whether or not SAEs are in this pathological regime in the wild.

papers.title: Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders for Monosemantic Representation
papers.research_question: How do concept activation distributions differ between Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and their base models, and do SAEs promote more monosemantic representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a distribution-aware concept separability score and shows that Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) reduce polysemanticity and achieve higher concept separability than their dense base models. It also proposes a new intervention method, Attenuation via Posterior Probabilities (APP), which enables effective concept removal with minimal side effects.
papers.conclusion: This work presents the first quantitative analysis of monosemanticity in SAEs compared to dense base models through a distributional lens, introduces a fine-grained concept separability score, and proposes a new intervention method (APP) that achieves effective concept removal with the least possible side effects.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs exhibit lower polysemanticity (neuron overlap) and higher concept separability than their base models across multiple datasets and models.
SAEs enable more precise concept-level interventions than base models, particularly when using partial suppression methods.
The proposed APP intervention method achieves the smallest perplexity increase while remaining highly competitive at concept removal.
Higher-capacity SAEs (e.g., 65k dimensions) yield greater concept separability and more effective interventions than lower-capacity ones.
A strong positive correlation exists between the concept separability score and the precision of partial concept erasure methods.
papers.limitation: APP uses a histogram-based approximation for density estimation to improve computational efficiency, which trades off accuracy and computational cost. Achieving the best possible performance requires significantly higher computational resources.
future_direction: Future work could explore alternative kernel density estimation (KDE) methods to better balance accuracy and efficiency for the APP method.
papers.abstract: A key barrier to interpreting large language models is polysemanticity, where neurons activate for multiple unrelated concepts. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have been proposed to mitigate this issue by transforming dense activations into sparse, more interpretable features. While prior work suggests that SAEs promote monosemanticity, no quantitative comparison has examined how concept activation distributions differ between SAEs and their base models. This paper provides the first systematic evaluation of SAEs against base models through activation distribution lens. We introduce a fine-grained concept separability score based on the Jensen-Shannon distance, which captures how distinctly a neuron's activation distributions vary across concepts. Using two large language models (Gemma-2-2B and DeepSeek-R1) and multiple SAE variants across five datasets (including word-level and sentence-level), we show that SAEs reduce polysemanticity and achieve higher concept separability. To assess practical utility, we evaluate concept-level interventions using two strategies: full neuron masking and partial suppression. We find that, compared to base models, SAEs enable more precise concept-level control when using partial suppression. Building on this, we propose Attenuation via Posterior Probabilities (APP), a new intervention method that uses concept-conditioned activation distributions for targeted suppression. APP achieves the smallest perplexity increase while remaining highly effective at concept removal.

papers.title: OrtSAE: Orthogonal Sparse Autoencoders Uncover Atomic Features
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate feature absorption and composition in sparse autoencoders to learn more atomic, interpretable features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces OrtSAE, a sparse autoencoder training method that enforces orthogonality between decoder features to reduce feature absorption and composition, yielding more atomic and interpretable features with minimal computational overhead.
papers.conclusion: OrtSAE effectively addresses feature absorption and composition in sparse autoencoders through orthogonal constraints, producing more atomic features while preserving reconstruction fidelity and downstream task performance with minimal computational overhead.
papers.key_findings:
OrtSAE discovers 9% more distinct features than traditional SAEs.
OrtSAE reduces feature absorption by 65% and feature composition by 15% compared to traditional SAEs.
OrtSAE improves performance on spurious correlation removal by 6% while maintaining on-par performance on other downstream tasks.
OrtSAE achieves feature orthogonality near random initialization levels, significantly lower than other SAE variants.
OrtSAE decomposes composite features from traditional SAEs into more atomic components, as shown qualitatively.
future_direction: Investigate using orthogonal features as more interpretable building blocks for neural circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a technique for sparse decomposition of neural network activations into human-interpretable features. However, current SAEs suffer from feature absorption, where specialized features capture instances of general features creating representation holes, and feature composition, where independent features merge into composite representations. In this work, we introduce Orthogonal SAE (OrtSAE), a novel approach aimed to mitigate these issues by enforcing orthogonality between the learned features. By implementing a new training procedure that penalizes high pairwise cosine similarity between SAE features, OrtSAE promotes the development of disentangled features while scaling linearly with the SAE size, avoiding significant computational overhead. We train OrtSAE across different models and layers and compare it with other methods. We find that OrtSAE discovers 9% more distinct features, reduces feature absorption (by 65%) and composition (by 15%), improves performance on spurious correlation removal (+6%), and achieves on-par performance for other downstream tasks compared to traditional SAEs.

papers.title: Transformer Key-Value Memories Are Nearly as Interpretable as Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: To what extent does a proxy-based, artificial decomposition of neuron activations (e.g., via sparse autoencoders) empirically benefit model interpretation compared to the organic features already represented within the original model's feed-forward layers?
papers.core_contribution: Features from feed-forward key-value memories (FF-KV) are nearly as interpretable as those from sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and in some aspects (e.g., absorption, explained variance) even outperform SAEs, suggesting that FF-KV features serve as a strong baseline for interpretability research.
papers.conclusion: Proxy-based methods such as SAEs offer very limited empirical advantage over direct analysis of feed-forward layers, and FF-KV features should be included as a strong baseline in interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
FF-KV features achieve comparable interpretability to SAE features across multiple automatic evaluation metrics from SAEBENCH.
FF-KV features sometimes outperform SAEs, e.g., in absorption (less redundancy) and explained variance (perfect by definition).
Human evaluation shows conceptual features can be found with almost equal ease from both FF-KV and SAEs.
Features discovered by proxy methods (e.g., Transcoders) often do not align with features in the original FF module, suggesting potential hallucination.
Increasing sparsity in FF-KV (via TopK) does not consistently improve interpretability across metrics.
papers.limitation:
SCR and TPP scores are highly unstable and should be treated as supplementary results.
The theoretical advantage of SAEs is not observed empirically through the current evaluation scheme.
future_direction: Further research on the faithfulness of learned features from proxy modules, with FF-KV features as grounding points.
Inclusion of FF-KV features as a baseline when assessing feature-discovery methods in interpretability.
papers.abstract: Recent interpretability work on large language models (LLMs) has been increasingly dominated by a feature-discovery approach with the help of proxy modules. Then, the quality of features learned by, e.g., sparse auto-encoders (SAEs), is evaluated. This paradigm naturally raises a critical question: do such learned features have better properties than those already represented within the original model parameters, and unfortunately, only a few studies have made such comparisons systematically so far. In this work, we revisit the interpretability of feature vectors stored in feed-forward (FF) layers, given the perspective of FF as key-value memories, with modern interpretability benchmarks. Our extensive evaluation revealed that SAE and FFs exhibits a similar range of interpretability, although SAEs displayed an observable but minimal improvement in some aspects. Furthermore, in certain aspects, surprisingly, even vanilla FFs yielded better interpretability than the SAEs, and features discovered in SAEs and FFs diverged. These bring questions about the advantage of SAEs from both perspectives of feature quality and faithfulness, compared to directly interpreting FF feature vectors, and FF key-value parameters serve as a strong baseline in modern interpretability research.

papers.title: Train One Sparse Autoencoder Across Multiple Sparsity Budgets to Preserve Interpretability and Accuracy
papers.research_question: How can a single sparse autoencoder be trained to maintain interpretability and accuracy across multiple sparsity levels, eliminating the need for separate models for each sparsity requirement?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces HierarchicalTopK, a novel training objective for sparse autoencoders that enables a single model to achieve Pareto-optimal trade-offs between sparsity and explained variance across multiple sparsity levels, while preserving interpretability.
papers.conclusion: HierarchicalTopK provides a flexible, efficient, and interpretable framework for analyzing Transformer latent spaces under varying computational constraints by training a single sparse autoencoder that works across multiple sparsity levels.
papers.key_findings:
The HierarchicalTopK SAE achieves Pareto-optimal trade-offs between sparsity and explained variance, matching or surpassing individually trained baseline SAEs across all sparsity levels.
The method maintains high interpretability scores (AutoInterp) across sparsity levels, unlike baseline SAEs where interpretability degrades at lower sparsity.
HierarchicalTopK prevents the proliferation of 'almost dead' features when the sparsity level (ℓ0) is reduced at inference time.
Computing the hierarchical loss on a subsampled set of indices (e.g., every 8th term) reduces theoretical FLOPs without sacrificing performance.
The proposed method provides a flexible and efficient framework for analyzing transformer latent spaces under varying computational constraints.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to the Gemma-2 2B model and a FineWeb subset; transfer to other architectures and datasets remains to be tested.
Reliance on automated metrics (AutoInterp) as proxies for human judgement; user studies are needed to validate semantic alignment.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have proven to be powerful tools for interpreting neural networks by decomposing hidden representations into disentangled, interpretable features via sparsity constraints. However, conventional SAEs are constrained by the fixed sparsity level chosen during training; meeting different sparsity requirements therefore demands separate models and increases the computational footprint during both training and evaluation. We introduce a novel training objective, \emph{HierarchicalTopK}, which trains a single SAE to optimise reconstructions across multiple sparsity levels simultaneously. Experiments with Gemma-2 2B demonstrate that our approach achieves Pareto-optimal trade-offs between sparsity and explained variance, outperforming traditional SAEs trained at individual sparsity levels. Further analysis shows that HierarchicalTopK preserves high interpretability scores even at higher sparsity. The proposed objective thus closes an important gap between flexibility and interpretability in SAE design.

papers.title: Can sparse autoencoders be used to decompose and interpret steering vectors?
papers.research_question: This paper investigates why directly applying sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to steering vectors yields misleading decompositions.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two main reasons why sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide misleading decompositions of steering vectors: (1) steering vectors are out-of-distribution for SAEs, and (2) SAEs cannot represent negative coefficients which are meaningful in steering vectors.
papers.conclusion: Direct SAE decomposition of steering vectors is misleading due to out-of-distribution and non-negativity constraints; alternative approaches such as learning steering vectors directly in the SAE basis are needed.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors have significantly smaller L2-norms than model activations, causing the SAE encoder bias to dominate the decomposition and yield misleading results.
Scaling steering vectors does not resolve the out-of-distribution issue because steering vectors lack default components present in model activations.
SAEs restrict decompositions to non-negative coefficients, but steering vectors have meaningful negative projections in feature directions.
Negative projections in steering vectors can cause spurious positive activations in SAE features due to negative cosine similarities between features.
These issues explain prior observations of irrelevant features in SAE decompositions and the failure of SAE-reconstructed vectors to retain steering properties.
papers.limitation:
The proposed alternative method of learning steering vectors directly in the SAE basis requires two SAE decompositions per difference vector, increasing the potential impact of SAE error.
The corrigibility steering vectors may include confounding features related to computer science and language modeling.
future_direction: Explore learning steering vectors directly in the SAE basis and establish evaluation metrics to compare with alternative methods.
papers.abstract: Steering vectors are a promising approach to control the behaviour of large language models. However, their underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. While sparse autoencoders (SAEs) may offer a potential method to interpret steering vectors, recent findings show that SAE-reconstructed vectors often lack the steering properties of the original vectors. This paper investigates why directly applying SAEs to steering vectors yields misleading decompositions, identifying two reasons: (1) steering vectors fall outside the input distribution for which SAEs are designed, and (2) steering vectors can have meaningful negative projections in feature directions, which SAEs are not designed to accommodate. These limitations hinder the direct use of SAEs for interpreting steering vectors.

papers.title: Data Whitening Improves Sparse Autoencoder Learning
papers.research_question: Does applying PCA whitening to input activations improve the interpretability of features learned by sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: PCA whitening significantly improves interpretability metrics of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) at a slight cost to reconstruction fidelity, by transforming the optimization landscape to be more convex and isotropic.
papers.conclusion: PCA whitening should be considered as a default preprocessing step for SAE training, especially when interpretability is prioritized over perfect reconstruction.
papers.key_findings:
Whitening transforms the SAE optimization landscape, making it more convex and isotropic, which improves feature recovery.
Whitening significantly improves interpretability metrics (sparse probing, SCR, TPP) for ReLU SAEs.
Whitening improves sparse probing for Top-K SAEs but does not significantly affect SCR or TPP.
Whitening causes a small but significant decrease in reconstruction quality (CE Loss and explained variance).
The benefits of whitening are more pronounced for ReLU-based SAEs than for Top-K SAEs.
papers.limitation: Experiments focus on middle layers of language models at the sub-2B parameter scale.
future_direction: Explore whitening's effects across different layers (early vs. late).
Investigate whitening on larger model scales (>2B parameters) and other architectures/modalities (vision, audio).
Study interactions between whitening and other training innovations (e.g., gated SAEs, transcoders).
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising approach for learning interpretable features from neural network activations. However, the optimization landscape for SAE training can be challenging due to correlations in the input data. We demonstrate that applying PCA Whitening to input activations -- a standard preprocessing technique in classical sparse coding -- improves SAE performance across multiple metrics. Through theoretical analysis and simulation, we show that whitening transforms the optimization landscape, making it more convex and easier to navigate. We evaluate both ReLU and Top-K SAEs across diverse model architectures, widths, and sparsity regimes. Empirical evaluation on SAEBench, a comprehensive benchmark for sparse autoencoders, reveals that whitening consistently improves interpretability metrics, including sparse probing accuracy and feature disentanglement, despite minor drops in reconstruction quality. Our results challenge the assumption that interpretability aligns with an optimal sparsity--fidelity trade-off and suggest that whitening should be considered as a default preprocessing step for SAE training, particularly when interpretability is prioritized over perfect reconstruction.

papers.title: AlignSAE: Concept-Aligned Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we align Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features with human-defined concepts to create an interpretable and controllable interface for Large Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: ALIGNSAE is a method that aligns Sparse Autoencoder features with a predefined ontology through a two-stage training curriculum, enabling precise concept-level inspection and control in frozen LLMs.
papers.conclusion: ALIGNSAE provides a verifiable and controllable interface for concept-level manipulation in LLMs, advancing interpretability and steering capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
ALIGNSAE achieves near-perfect concept-slot binding in mid-layers (e.g., layer 6) of GPT-2, with diagonal accuracy up to 1.00.
It significantly reduces concept fragmentation and increases top-1 concentration compared to traditional unsupervised SAEs.
Swap interventions demonstrate reliable controllability with a clear fidelity-strength tradeoff, achieving up to 0.847 swap success at layer 6.
In 2-hop reasoning, ALIGNSAE attains 4× higher swap success than traditional SAE.
The method provides mechanistic insights into grokking-like generalization dynamics via step-wise concept binding.
papers.limitation:
The method is evaluated on a limited ontology (6 relations for 1-hop, 20 for 2-hop) and on GPT-2, a relatively small model, which may not reflect performance on larger models or more complex ontologies.
Swap controllability has a narrow effective amplification range (around α=2), and over-amplification can destabilize interventions.
future_direction: Extending ALIGNSAE to larger ontologies and more complex concept types.
Applying the method to larger language models and more diverse tasks.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode factual knowledge within hidden parametric spaces that are difficult to inspect or control. While Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) can decompose hidden activations into more fine-grained, interpretable features, they often struggle to reliably align these features with human-defined concepts, resulting in entangled and distributed feature representations. To address this, we introduce AlignSAE, a method that aligns SAE features with a predefined ontology through a "pre-train, then post-train" curriculum. After an initial unsupervised training phase, we apply supervised post-training to bind specific concepts to dedicated latent slots while preserving the remaining capacity for general reconstruction. This separation creates an interpretable interface where specific concepts can be inspected and controlled without interference from unrelated features. Empirical results demonstrate that AlignSAE enables precise causal interventions, such as reliable "concept swaps", by targeting single, semantically aligned slots, and further supports multi-hop reasoning and a mechanistic probe of grokking-like generalization dynamics.

papers.title: Incorporating Hierarchical Semantics in Sparse Autoencoder Architectures
papers.research_question: Does incorporating hierarchical structure into sparse autoencoder architectures improve the reconstruction-interpretability frontier? Specifically, does it improve reconstruction, maintain or improve interpretability, and learn hierarchical semantics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a Hierarchical Sparse Autoencoder (H-SAE) architecture that explicitly models semantic hierarchy, improving reconstruction performance and interpretability while being computationally efficient.
papers.conclusion: Incorporating hierarchical structure into sparse autoencoder architectures improves the reconstruction-interpretability frontier, leading to better reconstruction, maintained or improved interpretability, and learned hierarchical semantics.
papers.key_findings:
H-SAEs have better reconstruction performance than standard SAEs as measured by explained variance and downstream CE loss.
H-SAEs maintain or improve interpretability, showing less feature absorption and fewer redundant features across languages.
The H-SAE architecture learns hierarchical semantics, with high-level features capturing general concepts and low-level features capturing specific instances.
The hierarchical structure provides significant computational efficiency gains, allowing scaling to larger effective dictionary sizes with minimal overhead.
The architecture successfully translates theoretical insights about hierarchical concept geometry into a practical mixture-of-experts type model.
papers.limitation: Results are still imperfect, with some hard-to-interpret features and far from perfect reconstruction.
future_direction: Explore other reconstruction objectives beyond Euclidean distance.
Incorporate insights from causal representation learning into LLM interpretability.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning (and, in particular, sparse autoencoders) attempts to learn a set of human-understandable concepts that can explain variation on an abstract space. A basic limitation of this approach is that it neither exploits nor represents the semantic relationships between the learned concepts. In this paper, we introduce a modified SAE architecture that explicitly models a semantic hierarchy of concepts. Application of this architecture to the internal representations of large language models shows both that semantic hierarchy can be learned, and that doing so improves both reconstruction and interpretability. Additionally, the architecture leads to significant improvements in computational efficiency.

papers.title: Group-SAE: Efficient Training of Sparse Autoencoders for Large Language Models via Layer Groups
papers.research_question: How can the computational cost of training Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for LLMs be reduced while maintaining performance? Specifically, can grouping similar layers and training a single SAE per group achieve this?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Group-SAE, a method to reduce the computational cost of training Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for LLMs by grouping layers with similar residual stream representations and training a single SAE per group, guided by a novel metric called AMAD (Average Maximum Angular Distance).
papers.conclusion: Group-SAE provides an efficient and scalable strategy for training SAEs in modern LLMs, achieving significant computational savings without compromising reconstruction quality, downstream task performance, or interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Group-SAE reduces the number of SAEs needed, cutting training costs by up to 50% with minimal impact on reconstruction quality and downstream performance.
The proposed AMAD metric effectively guides the selection of an optimal number of layer groups, balancing efficiency and performance.
Group-SAEs achieve comparable or slightly better interpretability scores (Detection and Fuzzing) than baseline per-layer SAEs.
Features learned by a Group-SAE are most similar to the baseline SAE trained on a layer within its group, and individual features typically peak at a specific layer but spread to adjacent ones.
The method outperforms alternative efficiency baselines like training smaller SAEs on all layers or using evenly spaced groups, especially on downstream performance metrics.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models from the Pythia family trained on the Pile dataset, and the generality to other architectures (e.g., Gemma, LLaMA) or datasets is not evaluated.
The study uses a fixed expansion factor (c=16) and TopK activation function; the impact of these hyperparameter choices is not investigated.
The interpretability evaluation is limited due to the high cost of annotating large numbers of features; a more comprehensive analysis is needed.
future_direction: Further optimizing the number of layer groups and scaling the approach to even larger models.
Evaluating the method on additional datasets and across diverse model architectures (e.g., Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen, Mistral).
Conducting a more comprehensive and systematic interpretability analysis.
papers.abstract: Sparse AutoEncoders (SAEs) have recently been employed as a promising unsupervised approach for understanding the representations of layers of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, with the growth in model size and complexity, training SAEs is computationally intensive, as typically one SAE is trained for each model layer. To address such limitation, we propose Group-SAE, a novel strategy to train SAEs. Our method considers the similarity of the residual stream representations between contiguous layers to group similar layers and train a single SAE per group. To balance the trade-off between efficiency and performance, we further introduce AMAD (Average Maximum Angular Distance), an empirical metric that guides the selection of an optimal number of groups based on representational similarity across layers. Experiments on models from the Pythia family show that our approach significantly accelerates training with minimal impact on reconstruction quality and comparable downstream task performance and interpretability over baseline SAEs trained layer by layer. This method provides an efficient and scalable strategy for training SAEs in modern LLMs.

papers.title: Feature Integration Spaces: Joint Training Reveals Dual Encoding in Neural Network Representations
papers.research_question: Does neural network encode information in two complementary spaces: feature identity and feature integration?
papers.core_contribution: This work provides systematic evidence for dual encoding in neural representations, meaningful nonlinearly encoded feature integrations, and introduces an architectural paradigm shift from post-hoc feature analysis to integrated computational design.
papers.conclusion: This work provides the first systematic evidence for dual-encoding spaces in neural network representations and introduces an architectural solution that achieves substantial improvements across multiple validation metrics, establishing foundations for next-generation SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Joint training achieves 41.3% reconstruction improvement and 51.6% reduction in KL divergence errors over SAE-only baseline.
The architecture spontaneously develops bimodal feature organization with low squared norm features specializing in integration pathways.
Integration features exhibit selective sensitivity to experimental manipulations and produce statistically significant nonlinear interaction effects on model outputs.
Nonlinear integration components achieve 16.5% standalone improvement using only 3% of parameters, demonstrating parameter efficiency.
Sequential SAE+NFM approach shows 23.4% error reduction and 29.8% reduction in pathological KL divergence errors.
papers.limitation:
Scale constraints represent one primary limitation of this work. Our experiments on a 3B parameter model with 50k SAE features provide proof-of-concept evidence, but scaling to industrial-scale models with millions of features is likely challenging.
Integration interpretability presents ongoing challenges. While we demonstrated functional effects, these features remain largely opaque to direct inspection.
Limitations of traditional feature discovery approaches, as maximum activation analysis on secondary features failed to yield interpretable patterns.
future_direction: Dynamic analysis of how integration patterns evolve during training
Cross-model validation
Cross-layer analysis
papers.abstract: Current sparse autoencoder (SAE) approaches to neural network interpretability assume that activations can be decomposed through linear superposition into sparse, interpretable features. Despite high reconstruction fidelity, SAEs consistently fail to eliminate polysemanticity and exhibit pathological behavioral errors. We propose that neural networks encode information in two complementary spaces compressed into the same substrate: feature identity and feature integration. To test this dual encoding hypothesis, we develop sequential and joint-training architectures to capture identity and integration patterns simultaneously. Joint training achieves 41.3% reconstruction improvement and 51.6% reduction in KL divergence errors. This architecture spontaneously develops bimodal feature organization: low squared norm features contributing to integration pathways and the rest contributing directly to the residual. Small nonlinear components (3% of parameters) achieve 16.5% standalone improvements, demonstrating parameter-efficient capture of computational relationships crucial for behavior. Additionally, intervention experiments using 2x2 factorial stimulus designs demonstrated that integration features exhibit selective sensitivity to experimental manipulations and produce systematic behavioral effects on model outputs, including significant statistical interaction effects across semantic dimensions. This work provides systematic evidence for (1) dual encoding in neural representations, (2) meaningful nonlinearly encoded feature interactions, and (3) introduces an architectural paradigm shift from post-hoc feature analysis to integrated computational design, establishing foundations for next-generation SAEs.

papers.title: Unveiling Latent Knowledge in Chemistry Language Models through Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How do chemistry language models internally represent chemical knowledge, and can sparse autoencoders uncover interpretable features within these models?
papers.core_contribution: This work presents the first application of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to chemistry language models, revealing that these models encode a rich hierarchy of interpretable chemical features spanning structural motifs, physicochemical properties, and functional concepts.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders can decompose the latent representations of a chemistry language model into an interpretable feature basis, revealing a rich landscape of chemically meaningful concepts and enabling causal manipulation of molecular structures.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features outperform individual neurons in detecting chemical substructures, especially rare ones, indicating a more disentangled representation.
SAE features provide a compact and decorrelated basis for aligning internal representations with external physicochemical descriptors.
Individual SAE features can capture higher-level functional concepts, such as grouping molecules by shared pharmacological activity (e.g., opioid receptor binding).
Feature steering via ablation demonstrates a causal link between specific features and the generation of corresponding chemical substructures or properties.
The SAE decomposition is information-preserving for downstream tasks (e.g., toxicity prediction) while isolating relevant signals into a more compact set of features than the original neuron basis.
papers.limitation:
The interpretation of features remains a presently unscaled process.
The analysis is confined to a single model architecture (SMI-TED).
The features discovered are contingent on the training data's chemical space, and their generalisation to out-of-distribution molecules remains an open question.
While features are compared to the raw neuron basis, more robust baselines are needed to fully validate the decomposition's effectiveness.
future_direction: Developing methods for the automated interpretation of chemical features.
Exploring applications in AI safety, such as identifying and ablating features correlated with undesirable properties (e.g., toxicity).
Investigating how features behave across different model architectures and scales, including exploring concepts like feature splitting.
papers.abstract: Since the advent of machine learning, interpretability has remained a persistent challenge, becoming increasingly urgent as generative models support high-stakes applications in drug and material discovery. Recent advances in large language model (LLM) architectures have yielded chemistry language models (CLMs) with impressive capabilities in molecular property prediction and molecular generation. However, how these models internally represent chemical knowledge remains poorly understood. In this work, we extend sparse autoencoder techniques to uncover and examine interpretable features within CLMs. Applying our methodology to the Foundation Models for Materials (FM4M) SMI-TED chemistry foundation model, we extract semantically meaningful latent features and analyse their activation patterns across diverse molecular datasets. Our findings reveal that these models encode a rich landscape of chemical concepts. We identify correlations between specific latent features and distinct domains of chemical knowledge, including structural motifs, physicochemical properties, and pharmacological drug classes. Our approach provides a generalisable framework for uncovering latent knowledge in chemistry-focused AI systems. This work has implications for both foundational understanding and practical deployment; with the potential to accelerate computational chemistry research.

papers.title: SAGE: Scalable Ground Truth Evaluations for Large Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate sparse autoencoders (SAEs) in the absence of ground truth features, and scale such evaluations to large models and tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAGE, a framework that enables scalable ground truth evaluation for sparse autoencoders by automatically discovering task-specific cross-sections and using residual stream SAEs to reduce training overhead.
papers.conclusion: SAGE enables large-scale SAE evaluations on realistic tasks, marking a significant advancement toward generalizable SAE assessments in interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
SAGE reproduces IOI evaluation results without prior knowledge, using only residual stream SAEs.
SAGE scales to new tasks (induction) and models (Pythia70M, GPT-2 Small, Gemma-2-2).
Larger SAEs (higher dimension) generally perform better in the evaluations.
Supervised feature dictionaries provide high-quality approximations of ground truth features, outperforming unsupervised SAEs in controllability.
The projection-based reconstruction method allows using residual stream SAEs for sublayer activations, reducing training overhead.
papers.limitation: The current approach is constrained by the effectiveness of attribution patching in identifying attribute cross-sections.
future_direction: Expanding task diversity by incorporating tasks with more high-level features and covering larger feature distributions.
Improving discovery methods for attribute cross-sections beyond attribution patching.
Incorporating additional activation disentanglement methods beyond SAEs, such as PCA or Distributed Alignment Search.
papers.abstract: A key challenge in interpretability is to decompose model activations into meaningful features. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising tool for this task. However, a central problem in evaluating the quality of SAEs is the absence of ground truth features to serve as an evaluation gold standard. Current evaluation methods for SAEs are therefore confronted with a significant trade-off: SAEs can either leverage toy models or other proxies with predefined ground truth features; or they use extensive prior knowledge of realistic task circuits. The former limits the generalizability of the evaluation results, while the latter limits the range of models and tasks that can be used for evaluations. We introduce SAGE: Scalable Autoencoder Ground-truth Evaluation, a ground truth evaluation framework for SAEs that scales to large state-of-the-art SAEs and models. We demonstrate that our method can automatically identify task-specific activations and compute ground truth features at these points. Compared to previous methods we reduce the training overhead by introducing a novel reconstruction method that allows to apply residual stream SAEs to sublayer activations. This eliminates the need for SAEs trained on every task-specific activation location. Then we validate the scalability of our framework, by evaluating SAEs on novel tasks on Pythia70M, GPT-2 Small, and Gemma-2-2. Our framework therefore paves the way for generalizable, large-scale evaluations of SAEs in interpretability research.

papers.title: Controllable LLM Reasoning via Sparse Autoencoder-Based Steering
papers.research_question: How can we control fine-grained reasoning strategies in Large Reasoning Models using Sparse Autoencoders to overcome concept entanglement and improve reliability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces SAE-Steering, a method that uses Sparse Autoencoders to disentangle and identify strategy-specific features for controlling reasoning strategies in Large Reasoning Models, achieving superior control effectiveness and error correction.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can disentangle strategy-specific features for fine-grained control of reasoning strategies, with SAE-Steering providing an efficient feature identification pipeline that is effective and robust.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-Steering outperforms existing control methods by over 15% in control effectiveness across various reasoning tasks and models.
The identified SAE features generalize from math to science domains, indicating cross-domain applicability.
Logit-based feature recall is more precise than activation-based methods, improving feature selection accuracy.
Strategy-specific features are prevalent in deeper layers of the model, with optimal control effectiveness in middle-to-late layers.
Controlling reasoning strategies can redirect models from erroneous paths, achieving a 7% absolute accuracy improvement in error correction.
papers.limitation:
Only evaluated five representative reasoning strategies
Only demonstrated application in error correction scenarios
Only attempted to correct erroneous paths by enforcing continued reasoning
future_direction: Investigate controlling other reasoning strategies
Explore applying control to a wider range of applications
Explore guiding the LRM at earlier stages or during intermediate steps
papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) exhibit human-like cognitive reasoning strategies (e.g. backtracking, cross-verification) during reasoning process, which improves their performance on complex tasks. Currently, reasoning strategies are autonomously selected by LRMs themselves. However, such autonomous selection often produces inefficient or even erroneous reasoning paths. To make reasoning more reliable and flexible, it is important to develop methods for controlling reasoning strategies. Existing methods struggle to control fine-grained reasoning strategies due to conceptual entanglement in LRMs' hidden states. To address this, we leverage Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to decompose strategy-entangled hidden states into a disentangled feature space. To identify the few strategy-specific features from the vast pool of SAE features, we propose SAE-Steering, an efficient two-stage feature identification pipeline. SAE-Steering first recalls features that amplify the logits of strategy-specific keywords, filtering out over 99\% of features, and then ranks the remaining features by their control effectiveness. Using the identified strategy-specific features as control vectors, SAE-Steering outperforms existing methods by over 15\% in control effectiveness. Furthermore, controlling reasoning strategies can redirect LRMs from erroneous paths to correct ones, achieving a 7\% absolute accuracy improvement.

papers.title: Explainable Autoencoder Deciphering Key Pathways Underlying Cancer Expression Patterns
papers.research_question: How to bridge the gap between complicated autoencoder models and biological interpretations for gene expression data, specifically to interpret the hidden variables learned by the autoencoder.
papers.core_contribution: Developed XAE4Exp, a tool that integrates autoencoder and SHAP to provide interpretable hidden variables for gene expression data, revealing pathways underlying breast cancer.
papers.conclusion: XAE4Exp is a helpful tool for interpreting AE-based data preprocessing and can lead to insightful knowledge on how to utilize the representations revealed by the AE-based machine learning.
papers.key_findings:
XAE4Exp can identify gene modules and pathways relevant to cancer pathogenesis, such as Spliceosome, Protein processing in endoplasmic reticulum, Oxidative phosphorylation.
XAE4Exp works even without control data (only cancer data), which is advantageous in medical data scarcity.
Compared to traditional methods like WGCNA and differential expression, XAE4Exp generates more accurate gene modules with corresponding weights.
papers.limitation:
Only DeepAE is used, but the tool could be extended to other AE structures such as Sparse AE, Denoising AE and Variational AE.
SHAP implementation is based on the Random Forest explainer, but other explainers such as Gradient Boosting Decision Tree (GBDT), CatBoost, etc., can also be incorporated.
The input data could be more abundant (only 1041 individuals), and performance might improve with more data.
future_direction: Extend to other AE structures such as Sparse AE, Denoising AE and Variational AE.
Incorporate other SHAP explainers such as Gradient Boosting Decision Tree (GBDT), CatBoost, etc.
Use more abundant input data to improve performance.
papers.abstract: Modern machine learning methods have been extensively utilized in gene expression data analysis. In particular, autoencoders (AE) have been employed in processing noisy and heterogenous RNA-Seq data. However, AEs usually lead to “black-box” hidden variables difficult to interpret, hindering downstream experimental validations and clinical translation. To bridge the gap between complicat-ed models and the biological interpretations, we developed a tool, XAE4Exp (eXplainable AutoEn-coder for Expression data), which integrates AE and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), a flagship technique in the field of eXplainable AI (XAI). It quantitatively evaluates the contributions of each gene to the hidden structure learned by an AE, substantially improving the expandability of AE outcomes. By applying XAE4Exp to The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) breast cancer gene ex-pression data, we revealed intriguing pathways including cell damage management, cell cycle, immune system related pathways underlying breast cancer. This tool will enable researchers and practitioners to analyze high-dimensional expression data intuitively, paving the way towards broad-er uses of deep learning.

papers.title: Open Roles In Interpretability Scaling Laws for Dictionary Learning Update on how we train SAEs How Strongly do Dictionary Learning Features Influence Model Behavior? Interpretability Architectures Project Caloric and the Utility of Incorrect Theories Open Problem: Attribution Dictionary Learning Isolating Circuits Paths of Different Lengths
papers.core_contribution: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.
papers.key_findings:
Scaling laws for dictionary learning show that loss decreases approximately as a power law with compute, with optimal allocations of training steps and features scaling as power laws.
An improved SAE training setup with modified loss function and initialization reduces loss and allows scaling to millions of features without issues.
Ablating dictionary learning features causes significantly more loss increase than random perturbations, indicating that features are high-leverage for model behavior.
Feature ablations have a larger effect than feature doublings, suggesting that feature influence may saturate at higher activations.
The impact of feature ablations is more pronounced for residual stream features compared to MLP features, hinting at different functional roles.
papers.limitation:
The relationship between SAE loss and qualitative usefulness of SAE features is imperfect and may break down at sufficient scale.
The SAE training initialization may need improvement and could cause issues for large feature counts.
The results on feature influence are preliminary and require further investigation.
future_direction: Exploring interpretable model architectures
Investigating attribution dictionary learning
Improving SAE training methods such as initialization and post-training
papers.abstract: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior. The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.

papers.title: Automated Interpretability Metrics Do Not Distinguish Trained and Random Transformers
papers.research_question: Do commonly used SAE quality metrics and automatic explanation pipelines distinguish trained transformers from randomly initialized ones?
papers.core_contribution: Common SAE metrics (e.g., auto-interpretability scores) do not reliably distinguish between trained and randomly initialized transformers, indicating these metrics are insufficient for validating interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: High aggregate auto-interpretability scores alone do not guarantee that learned, computationally relevant features have been recovered; the paper recommends routine randomized baselines and targeted measures of feature 'abstractness'.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on randomly initialized transformers produce auto-interpretability scores and reconstruction metrics similar to those from trained models.
Standard SAE quality metrics (explained variance, cosine similarity, L1 norm) show similar trends across trained and randomized variants.
Token distribution entropy reveals that features from randomized models remain simple and token-specific, unlike features from trained models which become more abstract across layers.
The area under the ROC curve (AUROC) for auto-interpretability tasks does not meaningfully discriminate between trained and randomized transformers in many settings.
Randomly initialized neural networks can preserve or amplify superposition present in input data, which may explain the similar SAE performance.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to Pythia models and the RedPajama dataset; results may vary with other architectures or data.
future_direction: Develop better metrics to distinguish between artifacts and genuinely learned computations in interpretability methods.
Investigate why randomly initialized transformers produce SAE metrics similar to trained ones, e.g., whether they preserve or amplify superposition.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used to extract sparse, interpretable latents from transformer activations. We test whether commonly used SAE quality metrics and automatic explanation pipelines can distinguish trained transformers from randomly initialized ones (e.g., where parameters are sampled i.i.d. from a Gaussian). Over a wide range of Pythia model sizes and multiple randomization schemes, we find that, in many settings, SAEs trained on randomly initialized transformers produce auto-interpretability scores and reconstruction metrics that are similar to those from trained models. These results show that high aggregate auto-interpretability scores do not, by themselves, guarantee that learned, computationally relevant features have been recovered. We therefore recommend treating common SAE metrics as useful but insufficient proxies for mechanistic interpretability and argue for routine randomized baselines and targeted measures of feature 'abstractness'.

papers.title: Transcoders Beat Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability
papers.research_question: Do transcoders and skip transcoders produce more interpretable features than sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for interpreting neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Skip transcoders Pareto-dominate SAEs on the tradeoff between reconstruction error and interpretability, and transcoders (including skip transcoders) produce more interpretable features than SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability researchers should shift their focus from sparse autoencoders trained on the outputs of MLPs to (skip) transcoders.
papers.key_findings:
Skip transcoders achieve lower reconstruction loss with no effect on interpretability compared to transcoders and SAEs.
Transcoders and skip transcoders have higher automated interpretability scores (fuzzing, detection, simulation) than SAEs.
The explanations for transcoder and skip transcoder latents are more accurate across the activation distribution and have a lower false positive rate.
Skip transcoders have lower cross-entropy loss increase when patched into the model compared to SAEs and transcoders.
Sparse probing performance is similar for skip transcoders and SAEs, with skip transcoders winning by a small margin in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Transcoders need to be trained on particular components of the model (usually a feedforward layer) and cannot be trained directly on the residual stream, though this can be mitigated by converting a skip transcoder to a 'residual stream transcoder'.
Feature absorption results are noisy and transcoders do not help improve the feature learning in SAEs the way new architectures do.
future_direction: Future work may illuminate the role of the skip connection by comparing it to a learned or analytically derived affine approximation of the MLP component.
Skip transcoders may be better for reconstructing circuits thanks to their lower reconstruction error, and future work could explore circuit analysis.

Transcoder and skip transcoder features may be used for steering, but benchmarks for unlearning and concept erasure require the latent to contain all information in any given residual stream position, which is not currently supported.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) extract human-interpretable features from deep neural networks by transforming their activations into a sparse, higher dimensional latent space, and then reconstructing the activations from these latents. Transcoders are similar to SAEs, but they are trained to reconstruct the output of a component of a deep network given its input. In this work, we compare the features found by transcoders and SAEs trained on the same model and data, finding that transcoder features are significantly more interpretable. We also propose skip transcoders, which add an affine skip connection to the transcoder architecture, and show that these achieve lower reconstruction loss with no effect on interpretability.

papers.title: XA4C: eXplainable representation learning via Autoencoders revealing Critical genes
papers.research_question: How can representation learning be made interpretable to prioritize critical genes from gene expression data?
papers.core_contribution: XA4C introduces an explainable autoencoder method to prioritize Critical genes from gene expression data, revealing novel biological insights not captured by traditional methods.
papers.conclusion: XA4C enables explainable representation learning for gene expression data, and Critical genes provide novel insights into disease pathways and complex interactions.
papers.key_findings:
Critical genes have little overlap with Hub or DiffEx genes, indicating they provide novel insights.
Critical genes have higher enrichment in disease databases like DisGeNET and COSMIC, showing strong relevance to pathology.
Critical genes capture essential cancer pathways such as oxidative phosphorylation and glutathione metabolism.
Critical genes show distinct interaction patterns in pathways like Lysine degradation between tumor and normal tissues.
XA4C outperforms traditional methods in terms of F1-score and precision when validated against DisGeNET.
papers.limitation:
Fixed architectures of autoencoders were used, which may not be optimal.
Only conventional autoencoders were used; other types like Variational AEs could be explored.
TreeSHAP was used instead of more efficient explainers like DeepSHAP.
Summarizing SHAP values over samples ignores individual heterogeneity.
XA4C currently supports only transcriptome data, not other omics data.
future_direction: Incorporate Bayesian Hyperparameter Optimization for autoencoder architectures.
Extend to other autoencoder types like Variational AE and Graph AE for causal inference.
Focus on individualized Critical genes to support precision medicine.
Incorporate additional omics data such as proteomics and metabolomics.
papers.abstract: Machine Learning models have been frequently used in transcriptome analyses. Particularly, Representation Learning (RL), e.g., autoencoders, are effective in learning critical representations in noisy data. However, learned representations, e.g., the "latent variables" in an autoencoder, are difficult to interpret, not to mention prioritizing essential genes for functional follow-up. In contrast, in traditional analyses, one may identify important genes such as Differentially Expressed (DiffEx), Differentially Co-Expressed (DiffCoEx), and Hub genes. Intuitively, the complex gene-gene interactions may be beyond the capture of marginal effects (DiffEx) or correlations (DiffCoEx and Hub), indicating the need of powerful RL models. However, the lack of interpretability and individual target genes is an obstacle for RL's broad use in practice. To facilitate interpretable analysis and gene-identification using RL, we propose "Critical genes", defined as genes that contribute highly to learned representations (e.g., latent variables in an autoencoder). As a proof-of-concept, supported by eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), we implemented eXplainable Autoencoder for Critical genes (XA4C) that quantifies each gene's contribution to latent variables, based on which Critical genes are prioritized. Applying XA4C to gene expression data in six cancers showed that Critical genes capture essential pathways underlying cancers. Remarkably, Critical genes has little overlap with Hub or DiffEx genes, however, has a higher enrichment in a comprehensive disease gene database (DisGeNET) and a cancer-specific database (COSMIC), evidencing its potential to disclose massive unknown biology. As an example, we discovered five Critical genes sitting in the center of Lysine degradation (hsa00310) pathway, displaying distinct interaction patterns in tumor and normal tissues. In conclusion, XA4C facilitates explainable analysis using RL and Critical genes discovered by explainable RL empowers the study of complex interactions.

papers.title: SynthSAEBench: Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders on Scalable Realistic Synthetic Data
papers.research_question: How can we create a scalable synthetic benchmark with ground-truth features to evaluate and diagnose Sparse Autoencoder architectures?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SynthSAEBench, a toolkit and benchmark for generating large-scale synthetic data with realistic feature characteristics (correlation, hierarchy, superposition) to evaluate and diagnose Sparse Autoencoder architectures.
papers.conclusion: SynthSAEBench complements LLM benchmarks by providing ground-truth features and controlled ablations, enabling precise diagnosis of SAE failure modes and validation of architectural improvements before scaling to LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Reproduces LLM SAE phenomena: Matryoshka SAEs overperform on probing despite poor reconstruction; MP-SAEs overperform on reconstruction but poor probing; poor SAE probing relative to supervised probes; precision-recall trade-off mediated by L0.
Identifies a new failure mode: MP-SAEs exploit superposition noise to improve reconstruction without learning ground-truth features, suggesting expressive encoders can overfit.
No SAE architecture achieves perfect performance on SynthSAEBench-16k, highlighting a target for architectural improvement.
papers.limitation: The synthetic model cannot capture all aspects of real neural network representations.
future_direction: Extend the framework to Minkowski representations and feature manifolds.
Understand the performance gap between JumpReLU and BatchTopK SAEs.
papers.abstract: Improving Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) requires benchmarks that can precisely validate architectural innovations. However, current SAE benchmarks on LLMs are often too noisy to differentiate architectural improvements, and current synthetic data experiments are too small-scale and unrealistic to provide meaningful comparisons. We introduce SynthSAEBench, a toolkit for generating large-scale synthetic data with realistic feature characteristics including correlation, hierarchy, and superposition, and a standardized benchmark model, SynthSAEBench-16k, enabling direct comparison of SAE architectures. Our benchmark reproduces several previously observed LLM SAE phenomena, including the disconnect between reconstruction and latent quality metrics, poor SAE probing results, and a precision-recall trade-off mediated by L0. We further use our benchmark to identify a new failure mode: Matching Pursuit SAEs exploit superposition noise to improve reconstruction without learning ground-truth features, suggesting that more expressive encoders can easily overfit.
