SynthSAEBench complements LLM benchmarks by providing ground-truth features and controlled ablations, enabling researchers to precisely diagnose SAE failure modes and validate architectural improvements before scaling to LLMs.

papers.title: Teach Old SAEs New Domain Tricks with Boosting
papers.research_question: How can we address feature blindness in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for domain-specific interpretability without requiring complete retraining?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAE Boost, a residual learning approach that trains a secondary SAE to model the reconstruction error of a pretrained SAE on domain-specific texts, enabling selective enhancement of interpretability for specialized domains without full retraining.
papers.conclusion: SAE Boost addresses feature blindness in SAEs, enabling selective domain enhancement without modifying the base model, and represents an important step forward in targeted mechanistic interpretability of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
SAE Boost significantly improves explained variance and LLM cross-entropy on domain-specific texts compared to a pretrained SAE alone.
The method maintains general domain performance with minimal degradation, confirming it learns complementary features.
SAE Boost captures domain-specific features that general-purpose SAEs miss, as shown by interpretability analysis and lower cosine similarity to base features.
The approach is modular, allowing multiple domain-specific residual SAEs to be applied simultaneously without compromising performance.
SAE Boost outperforms alternative domain adaptation methods like Extended SAE and SAE Stitching in balancing domain performance, general performance, and sparsity.
papers.limitation:
Undertraining the residual SAE (e.g., on fewer than 100M tokens) can degrade general domain performance by up to 31% in explained variance.
Early stopping based solely on domain-specific metrics may lead to suboptimal feature quality.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders have emerged as powerful tools for interpreting the internal representations of Large Language Models, yet they often fail to capture domain-specific features not prevalent in their training corpora. This paper introduces a residual learning approach that addresses this feature blindness without requiring complete retraining. We propose training a secondary SAE specifically to model the reconstruction error of a pretrained SAE on domain-specific texts, effectively capturing features missed by the primary model. By summing the outputs of both models during inference, we demonstrate significant improvements in both LLM cross-entropy and explained variance metrics across multiple specialized domains. Our experiments show that this method efficiently incorporates new domain knowledge into existing SAEs while maintaining their performance on general tasks. This approach enables researchers to selectively enhance SAE interpretability for specific domains of interest, opening new possibilities for targeted mechanistic interpretability of LLMs.

papers.title: Evaluating Open-Source Sparse Autoencoders on Disentangling Factual Knowledge in GPT-2 Small
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoder (SAE) feature spaces are useful for causal interpretability analysis, specifically for disentangling related factual knowledge (country and continent of cities) in language models.
papers.core_contribution: Current open-source sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for GPT-2 small struggle to provide a feature space that better disentangles factual knowledge than the baseline of neurons, and none approach the performance of the supervised DAS skyline.
papers.conclusion: Only one of the evaluated SAEs reached the neuron baseline and none reached the DAS skyline, indicating current SAEs are not superior to neurons for this causal disentanglement task, but the evaluation is a useful step for assessing SAEs in interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Using representations reconstructed by SAEs degrades the model's knowledge of cities.
The end-to-end SAEs degrade knowledge less relative to their reconstruction loss, but this is weak evidence.
There is a significant gap between the neuron baseline and the DAS skyline, showing neurons can be improved upon.
Current SAEs for GPT-2 small generally perform below the neuron baseline, with only the top-k Open AI SAE matching it.
The top-k SAE (Open AI SAE) is the most performant among the evaluated SAEs.
papers.limitation: The evaluation is limited to GPT-2 small and a specific dataset (cities, countries, continents). Future work should scale to larger models and more attributes.
future_direction: Scale experiments to models with available SAEs including gemma, Mistral, Llama, and Pythia.
Use more attributes from the RA VEL dataset, such as language, gender, etc., for larger models with more knowledge.
papers.abstract: A popular new method in mechanistic interpretability is to train high-dimensional sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on neuron activations and use SAE features as the atomic units of analysis. However, the body of evidence on whether SAE feature spaces are useful for causal analysis is underdeveloped. In this work, we use the RAVEL benchmark to evaluate whether SAEs trained on hidden representations of GPT-2 small have sets of features that separately mediate knowledge of which country a city is in and which continent it is in. We evaluate four open-source SAEs for GPT-2 small against each other, with neurons serving as a baseline, and linear features learned via distributed alignment search (DAS) serving as a skyline. For each, we learn a binary mask to select features that will be patched to change the country of a city without changing the continent, or vice versa. Our results show that SAEs struggle to reach the neuron baseline, and none come close to the DAS skyline. We release code here: https://github.com/MaheepChaudhary/SAE-Ravel

papers.title: Measuring and Guiding Monosemanticity
papers.research_question: How can we systematically measure and improve the monosemanticity (single-concept encoding) of feature representations in large language models, specifically within Sparse Autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric for quantifying monosemanticity in latent representations, and proposes Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that uses latent conditioning during training to enforce isolated, monosemantic feature representations, improving interpretability and control.
papers.conclusion: The introduced FMS metric and G-SAE method provide actionable guidelines for advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs by enabling reliable measurement and enforcement of monosemantic feature representations.
papers.key_findings:
G-SAE achieves significantly higher FMS scores than vanilla SAEs, indicating stronger feature monosemanticity, localization, and disentanglement.
G-SAE enables more effective and precise concept detection (e.g., toxicity, writing style, privacy attributes) compared to unsupervised SAEs.
Steering using G-SAE's decoder vectors allows for fine-grained control over model outputs (e.g., reducing toxicity, altering writing style) with less quality degradation than baseline methods.
The proposed FMS metric reveals critical shortcomings in the monosemanticity of features learned by standard, unsupervised SAEs.
papers.limitation:
The training of G-SAE requires labeled data for the target concepts, which may not always be available.
The method could be misused for adversarial steering to amplify undesirable model behaviors.
papers.abstract: There is growing interest in leveraging mechanistic interpretability and controllability to better understand and influence the internal dynamics of large language models (LLMs). However, current methods face fundamental challenges in reliably localizing and manipulating feature representations. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a promising direction for feature extraction at scale, yet they, too, are limited by incomplete feature isolation and unreliable monosemanticity. To systematically quantify these limitations, we introduce Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric to quantify feature monosemanticity in latent representation. Building on these insights, we propose Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that conditions latent representations on labeled concepts during training. We demonstrate that reliable localization and disentanglement of target concepts within the latent space improve interpretability, detection of behavior, and control. Specifically, our evaluations on toxicity detection, writing style identification, and privacy attribute recognition show that G-SAE not only enhances monosemanticity but also enables more effective and fine-grained steering with less quality degradation. Our findings provide actionable guidelines for measuring and advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs.

papers.title: AdaptiveK Sparse Autoencoders: Dynamic Sparsity Allocation for Interpretable LLM Representations
papers.research_question: How can we define semantic simplicity or complexity within LLM representation spaces, and how can this be used to dynamically adjust sparsity in sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AdaptiveK SAE, a sparse autoencoder framework that dynamically adjusts sparsity levels based on input complexity, improving reconstruction and interpretability without extensive hyperparameter tuning.
papers.conclusion: AdaptiveK SAE provides an efficient and effective method for interpretable feature extraction in LLMs by dynamically allocating sparsity based on input complexity.
papers.key_findings:
Text complexity is linearly encoded in LLM representations, as demonstrated by linear probes.
Adaptive sparsity allocation based on complexity improves reconstruction quality and interpretability metrics across multiple model scales.
AdaptiveK SAE outperforms fixed-sparsity baselines on reconstruction fidelity, explained variance, and cosine similarity.
papers.limitation: Due to cost constraints, the study used a smaller training dataset (250,000 contexts) compared to the 500,000,000 tokens used in SAEBench.
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal representations of large language models (LLMs) remains a central challenge for interpretability research. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) offer a promising solution by decomposing activations into interpretable features, but existing approaches rely on fixed sparsity constraints that fail to account for input complexity. We propose AdaptiveK SAE (Adaptive Top K Sparse Autoencoders), a novel framework that dynamically adjusts sparsity levels based on the semantic complexity of each input. Leveraging linear probes, we demonstrate that context complexity is linearly encoded in LLM representations, and we use this signal to guide feature allocation during training. Experiments across ten language models (from 70M to 14B parameters) demonstrate that this complexity-driven adaptation significantly outperforms fixed-sparsity approaches on reconstruction fidelity, explained variance, cosine similarity and interpretability metrics while eliminating the computational burden of extensive hyperparameter tuning.

papers.title: Llama Scope: Extracting Millions of Features from Llama-3.1-8B with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we scalably train Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) on large language models, and how do these SAEs perform in terms of sparsity-fidelity trade-off, interpretability, and generalization to longer contexts and fine-tuned models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Llama Scope, a suite of 256 Sparse Autoencoders trained on every layer and sublayer of Llama-3.1-8B-Base, along with modifications to Top-K SAEs and a scalable training infrastructure, providing a resource for mechanistic interpretability research.
papers.conclusion: Llama Scope provides a comprehensive set of SAEs that advance the Pareto frontier of sparsity and reconstruction fidelity, and the SAEs generalize effectively to out-of-distribution settings, facilitating future interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
TopK SAEs outperform vanilla SAEs in sparsity-fidelity trade-off.
Wider SAEs (with more features) achieve better reconstruction quality at the same sparsity level.
SAEs trained on base models generalize well to longer contexts and instruction-finetuned models.
Feature geometry analysis confirms that feature splitting enables the discovery of new features.
The firing frequency distribution of SAE features is consistent with expected sparsity constraints.
papers.limitation:
The monosemanticity evaluation focuses on top activations and may not capture behavior on low-activating samples.
The online activation generation method can lead to redundant computation when training multiple SAEs on the same position.
future_direction: Exploring SAE-based circuit analysis and fine-grained causal analysis.
Conducting automated prompt-based evaluations across a wide range of tasks.
Fine-tuning SAEs for long-context data.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful unsupervised method for extracting sparse representations from language models, yet scalable training remains a significant challenge. We introduce a suite of 256 SAEs, trained on each layer and sublayer of the Llama-3.1-8B-Base model, with 32K and 128K features. Modifications to a state-of-the-art SAE variant, Top-K SAEs, are evaluated across multiple dimensions. In particular, we assess the generalizability of SAEs trained on base models to longer contexts and fine-tuned models. Additionally, we analyze the geometry of learned SAE latents, confirming that \emph{feature splitting} enables the discovery of new features. The Llama Scope SAE checkpoints are publicly available at~\url{https://huggingface.co/fnlp/Llama-Scope}, alongside our scalable training, interpretation, and visualization tools at \url{https://github.com/OpenMOSS/Language-Model-SAEs}. These contributions aim to advance the open-source Sparse Autoencoder ecosystem and support mechanistic interpretability research by reducing the need for redundant SAE training.

papers.title: Interpreting and Steering LLMs with Mutual Information-based Explanations on Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How to better explain sparse autoencoder features in LLMs to capture semantic meaning and use these explanations to steer LLM behaviors, particularly for defending against jailbreak attacks.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a mutual information-based explanation method for sparse autoencoder features that mitigates frequency bias and enables effective steering of LLM behaviors, particularly for enhancing safety against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that discourse-level explanations from sparse autoencoders are crucial for understanding and steering LLM behaviors, particularly for safety applications.
papers.key_findings:
Theoretical analysis reveals frequency bias in sparse autoencoder features between discourse topics and linguistic patterns.
The proposed mutual information-based method generates more discourse-level explanations compared to baseline methods like TopAct and N2G.
The discourse-level explanations are effective in steering LLM behaviors to defend against jailbreak attacks.
Experiments show a higher successful explained rate for features with the proposed method.
Steering strategies such as amplification and calibration can enhance LLM safety without additional model training.
papers.limitation: The approach relies on existing sparse autoencoders without modifying their architectures or training to mitigate frequency bias.
future_direction: Designing improved architectures or training objectives for sparse autoencoders to inherently mitigate frequency bias.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at handling human queries, but they can occasionally generate flawed or unexpected responses. Understanding their internal states is crucial for understanding their successes, diagnosing their failures, and refining their capabilities. Although sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promise for interpreting LLM internal representations, limited research has explored how to better explain SAE features, i.e., understanding the semantic meaning of features learned by SAE. Our theoretical analysis reveals that existing explanation methods suffer from the frequency bias issue, where they emphasize linguistic patterns over semantic concepts, while the latter is more critical to steer LLM behaviors. To address this, we propose using a fixed vocabulary set for feature interpretations and designing a mutual information-based objective, aiming to better capture the semantic meaning behind these features. We further propose two runtime steering strategies that adjust the learned feature activations based on their corresponding explanations. Empirical results show that, compared to baselines, our method provides more discourse-level explanations and effectively steers LLM behaviors to defend against jailbreak attacks. These findings highlight the value of explanations for steering LLM behaviors in downstream applications. We will release our code and data once accepted.

papers.title: Improving Dictionary Learning with Gated Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be improved to reduce biases like shrinkage and achieve better sparsity and reconstruction fidelity in language model activations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Gated SAEs that decouple feature detection and magnitude estimation, solving shrinkage and providing Pareto improvements in sparsity and reconstruction fidelity over baseline SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Gated SAEs are a promising improvement for sparse autoencoders in mechanistic interpretability, offering better performance and reduced biases.
papers.key_findings:
Gated SAEs achieve better reconstruction fidelity at any given level of sparsity compared to baseline SAEs.
Gated SAEs effectively address the shrinkage problem, with reconstructions being unbiased.
Gated SAE features are similarly interpretable to baseline SAE features based on human evaluation.
Ablation studies show that freezing the decoder in the auxiliary task and weight tying are important for performance.
papers.abstract: Recent work has found that sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are an effective technique for unsupervised discovery of interpretable features in language models' (LMs) activations, by finding sparse, linear reconstructions of LM activations. We introduce the Gated Sparse Autoencoder (Gated SAE), which achieves a Pareto improvement over training with prevailing methods. In SAEs, the L1 penalty used to encourage sparsity introduces many undesirable biases, such as shrinkage -- systematic underestimation of feature activations. The key insight of Gated SAEs is to separate the functionality of (a) determining which directions to use and (b) estimating the magnitudes of those directions: this enables us to apply the L1 penalty only to the former, limiting the scope of undesirable side effects. Through training SAEs on LMs of up to 7B parameters we find that, in typical hyper-parameter ranges, Gated SAEs solve shrinkage, are similarly interpretable, and require half as many firing features to achieve comparable reconstruction fidelity.

papers.title: Training Superior Sparse Autoencoders for Instruct Models
papers.research_question: How can we effectively train sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on instruct models, given that existing methods designed for base models result in reduced reconstruction quality and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Finetuning-aligned Sequential Training (FAST), a novel method for training sparse autoencoders on instruct models that aligns the training process with the data distribution and activation patterns of instruct models, leading to significant improvements in reconstruction quality and feature interpretability.
papers.conclusion: FAST is an effective method for training SAEs on instruct models, achieving superior reconstruction and feature interpretability, and the resulting SAEs can be used to steer model behavior via special token features, opening new avenues for model control.
papers.key_findings:
FAST significantly outperforms baseline Block Training methods (BT(P) and BT(F)) in token reconstruction (MSE) and special token reconstruction (MSEst) across multiple instruct models and SAE architectures.
FAST produces a higher proportion of high-quality, interpretable features compared to baseline methods, as measured by an automated feature interpretability scoring framework.
Intervening on the activations of special tokens via the trained SAEs can improve output quality and enable fine-grained control of model behavior, suggesting new applications for SAEs.
future_direction: Exploring the opportunities for fine-grained control of model behavior through steering with SAE latents, particularly via special tokens.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) grow in scale and capability, understanding their internal mechanisms becomes increasingly critical. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a key tool in mechanistic interpretability, enabling the extraction of human-interpretable features from LLMs. However, existing SAE training methods are primarily designed for base models, resulting in reduced reconstruction quality and interpretability when applied to instruct models. To bridge this gap, we propose $\underline{\textbf{F}}$inetuning-$\underline{\textbf{a}}$ligned $\underline{\textbf{S}}$equential $\underline{\textbf{T}}$raining ($\textit{FAST}$), a novel training method specifically tailored for instruct models. $\textit{FAST}$ aligns the training process with the data distribution and activation patterns characteristic of instruct models, resulting in substantial improvements in both reconstruction and feature interpretability. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, $\textit{FAST}$ achieves a mean squared error of 0.6468 in token reconstruction, significantly outperforming baseline methods with errors of 5.1985 and 1.5096. In feature interpretability, $\textit{FAST}$ yields a higher proportion of high-quality features, for Llama3.2-3B-Instruct, $21.1\%$ scored in the top range, compared to $7.0\%$ and $10.2\%$ for $\textit{BT(P)}$ and $\textit{BT(F)}$. Surprisingly, we discover that intervening on the activations of special tokens via the SAEs leads to improvements in output quality, suggesting new opportunities for fine-grained control of model behavior. Code, data, and 240 trained SAEs are available at https://github.com/Geaming2002/FAST.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Enable Scalable and Reliable Circuit Identification in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently and robustly discover interpretable circuits in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method for circuit identification using discrete sparse autoencoders trained on attention head outputs, which is more efficient and robust than existing techniques.
papers.conclusion: Discrete sparse autoencoders offer a scalable, efficient, and robust approach for circuit identification in large language models, providing a promising direction for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The method outperforms or matches state-of-the-art circuit identification techniques (ACDC, HISP, SP) in precision and recall on three tasks (IOI, Greater-than, Docstring).
The method is robust to hyperparameter choices and requires only 5-10 text examples per task to learn robust representations.
The identified circuits can match or even outperform the full model's performance on the specific tasks with fewer components.
The method can identify negative components in circuits (e.g., negative name-mover heads in IOI) that other algorithms struggle to find.
The process is significantly faster, reducing runtime from hours to seconds compared to existing methods.
papers.limitation: The method currently only analyzes attention heads and not other components like MLP layers, which may be important for some circuits (e.g., Greater-than).
future_direction: Extending the method to analyze MLP layers and other model components.
Applying the method to larger models and more complex tasks.
Exploring the use of vector-quantized variational autoencoders (VQ-VAEs) as an alternative to sparse autoencoders.
papers.abstract: This paper introduces an efficient and robust method for discovering interpretable circuits in large language models using discrete sparse autoencoders. Our approach addresses key limitations of existing techniques, namely computational complexity and sensitivity to hyperparameters. We propose training sparse autoencoders on carefully designed positive and negative examples, where the model can only correctly predict the next token for the positive examples. We hypothesise that learned representations of attention head outputs will signal when a head is engaged in specific computations. By discretising the learned representations into integer codes and measuring the overlap between codes unique to positive examples for each head, we enable direct identification of attention heads involved in circuits without the need for expensive ablations or architectural modifications. On three well-studied tasks - indirect object identification, greater-than comparisons, and docstring completion - the proposed method achieves higher precision and recall in recovering ground-truth circuits compared to state-of-the-art baselines, while reducing runtime from hours to seconds. Notably, we require only 5-10 text examples for each task to learn robust representations. Our findings highlight the promise of discrete sparse autoencoders for scalable and efficient mechanistic interpretability, offering a new direction for analysing the inner workings of large language models.

papers.title: Temporal Sparse Autoencoders: Leveraging the Sequential Nature of Language for Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we incorporate temporal consistency into sparse autoencoders to better recover high-level semantic features in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Temporal Sparse Autoencoders (T-SAEs) that incorporate a temporal contrastive loss to encourage consistent activations of high-level features over adjacent tokens, leading to better disentanglement of semantic and syntactic features in language models.
papers.conclusion: Temporal SAEs leverage the sequential nature of language to better extract semantic features, offering a new pathway for unsupervised interpretability in language models.
papers.key_findings:
T-SAEs recover smoother, more coherent semantic concepts without sacrificing reconstruction quality.
T-SAEs exhibit clear semantic structure despite being trained without explicit semantic signal.
T-SAEs show improved disentanglement between high-level (semantic) and low-level (syntactic) features.
T-SAEs provide practical interpretability benefits, such as in safety monitoring and steering.
papers.abstract: Translating the internal representations and computations of models into concepts that humans can understand is a key goal of interpretability. While recent dictionary learning methods such as Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) provide a promising route to discover human-interpretable features, they suffer from a variety of problems, including a systematic failure to capture the rich conceptual information that drives linguistic understanding. Instead, they exhibit a bias towards shallow, token-specific, or noisy features, such as "the phrase 'The' at the start of sentences". In this work, we propose that this is due to a fundamental issue with how dictionary learning methods for LLMs are trained. Language itself has a rich, well-studied structure spanning syntax, semantics, and pragmatics; however, current unsupervised methods largely ignore this linguistic knowledge, leading to poor feature discovery that favors superficial patterns over meaningful concepts. We focus on a simple but important aspect of language: semantic content has long-range dependencies and tends to be smooth over a sequence, whereas syntactic information is much more local. Building on this insight, we introduce Temporal Sparse Autoencoders (T-SAEs), which incorporate a novel contrastive loss encouraging consistent activations of high-level features over adjacent tokens. This simple yet powerful modification enables SAEs to disentangle semantic from syntactic features in a self-supervised manner. Across multiple datasets and models, T-SAEs recover smoother, more coherent semantic concepts without sacrificing reconstruction quality. Strikingly, they exhibit clear semantic structure despite being trained without explicit semantic signal, offering a new pathway for unsupervised interpretability in language models.

papers.title: MedSAE: Dissecting MedCLIP Representations with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to improve interpretability of medical vision-language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Medical Sparse Autoencoders (MedSAEs) to extract interpretable, monosemantic features from MedCLIP embeddings, advancing mechanistic interpretability in medical vision.
papers.conclusion: This work presents a first step toward mechanistic interpretability in medical vision-language models, highlighting sparse autoencoders as a promising direction for building transparent, robust, and trustworthy medical AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
MedSAE neurons achieve lower entropy (2.25) than raw MedCLIP features (2.38), indicating higher monosemanticity.
21 medically meaningful features are identified with MedGEMMA-based automated naming, with detection accuracy above 70%.
MedSAE features show stronger alignment with clinical concepts compared to raw embeddings.
papers.limitation:
presence of inactive neurons and the need for more expressive SAE architectures
computational cost and dataset sensitivity of automated naming
limited validation across modalities and institutions
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence in healthcare requires models that are accurate and interpretable. We advance mechanistic interpretability in medical vision by applying Medical Sparse Autoencoders (MedSAEs) to the latent space of MedCLIP, a vision-language model trained on chest radiographs and reports. To quantify interpretability, we propose an evaluation framework that combines correlation metrics, entropy analyzes, and automated neuron naming via the MedGEMMA foundation model. Experiments on the CheXpert dataset show that MedSAE neurons achieve higher monosemanticity and interpretability than raw MedCLIP features. Our findings bridge high-performing medical AI and transparency, offering a scalable step toward clinically reliable representations.

papers.title: Decomposing The Dark Matter of Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What is the structure of SAE error (dark matter)? Can SAE error be predicted from activations? How do the linearly predictable and nonlinearly predictable components differ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that SAE error (dark matter) is largely linearly predictable from model activations, and that the nonlinear component is qualitatively different, containing fewer not-yet-learned features and being harder to learn.
papers.conclusion: The fact that SAE error can be predicted and analyzed is surprising, indicating SAE errors are worthy of analysis. The presence of constant nonlinear error at fixed sparsity suggests scaling SAEs may not be the only way to explain more of model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
SAE error norms and vectors can be linearly predicted from activations with high accuracy (R2 between 70-95% for norms, 15-72% for vectors).
The scaling behavior of SAE error norms is predictable across different SAE sizes; larger SAEs struggle to reconstruct the same contexts as smaller SAEs.
The nonlinear component of SAE error contains fewer not-yet-learned features, is harder to learn SAEs for, and contributes proportionally to cross entropy loss.
Inference time gradient pursuit reduces total FVU by 3-5% but leaves nonlinear error mostly unchanged.
Linear transformations from earlier layer SAE outputs can reduce nonlinear error and total SAE error.
future_direction: Explore alternative penalties besides sparsity or new ways to learn better dictionaries.
Incorporate low-rank dense side channels in SAE architecture.
Use small-scale trials to forecast SAE scaling behavior.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a promising technique for decomposing language model activations into interpretable linear features. However, current SAEs fall short of completely explaining model performance, resulting in "dark matter": unexplained variance in activations. This work investigates dark matter as an object of study in its own right. Surprisingly, we find that much of SAE dark matter -- about half of the error vector itself and >90% of its norm -- can be linearly predicted from the initial activation vector. Additionally, we find that the scaling behavior of SAE error norms at a per token level is remarkably predictable: larger SAEs mostly struggle to reconstruct the same contexts as smaller SAEs. We build on the linear representation hypothesis to propose models of activations that might lead to these observations. These insights imply that the part of the SAE error vector that cannot be linearly predicted ("nonlinear" error) might be fundamentally different from the linearly predictable component. To validate this hypothesis, we empirically analyze nonlinear SAE error and show that 1) it contains fewer not yet learned features, 2) SAEs trained on it are quantitatively worse, and 3) it is responsible for a proportional amount of the downstream increase in cross entropy loss when SAE activations are inserted into the model. Finally, we examine two methods to reduce nonlinear SAE error: inference time gradient pursuit, which leads to a very slight decrease in nonlinear error, and linear transformations from earlier layer SAE outputs, which leads to a larger reduction.

papers.title: Interpretability as Compression: Reconsidering SAE Explanations of Neural Activations with MDL-SAEs
papers.research_question: How can we use the Minimal Description Length principle to train and select Sparse Autoencoders that provide concise and interpretable explanations of neural activations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an information-theoretic framework that views SAEs as lossy compression algorithms for neural activations, using the Minimal Description Length principle to select SAEs that provide concise and interpretable explanations, and introduces the property of independent additivity for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the MDL principle provides a theoretical motivation for SAE architectures and hyperparameters, and can help in creating principled evaluations for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can be viewed as communication protocols for transmitting neural activations, and the MDL principle can be used to select SAEs that balance accuracy and conciseness.
Interpretability requires independent additivity, meaning features should be understandable separately.
On MNIST, MDL-SAEs find stroke-like features that are more interpretable and composable than features from very sparse or dense SAEs.
Optimizing for MDL can reduce undesirable feature splitting compared to optimizing for sparsity alone.
Hierarchical feature structures can lead to more efficient coding schemes and lower description length.
papers.limitation: The MDL principle is treated as a strategy for model selection: to choose a model out of a collection of multiple models. However, training multiple models with a hyperparameter sweep may be computationally expensive.
future_direction: Future work could look to include the entropy term in the loss function and optimise for it directly through either a straight-thought estimation approach or with a Bayesian prior.

Future work could explore to what extent variants in SAE architectures can decrease the MDL of communicated latent feature activations, and exploiting causal structure inherent in the data distribution may be important to efficient coding.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a useful tool for interpreting the internal representations of neural networks. However, naively optimising SAEs for reconstruction loss and sparsity results in a preference for SAEs that are extremely wide and sparse. We present an information-theoretic framework for interpreting SAEs as lossy compression algorithms for communicating explanations of neural activations. We appeal to the Minimal Description Length (MDL) principle to motivate explanations of activations which are both accurate and concise. We further argue that interpretable SAEs require an additional property, "independent additivity": features should be able to be understood separately. We demonstrate an example of applying our MDL-inspired framework by training SAEs on MNIST handwritten digits and find that SAE features representing significant line segments are optimal, as opposed to SAEs with features for memorised digits from the dataset or small digit fragments. We argue that using MDL rather than sparsity may avoid potential pitfalls with naively maximising sparsity such as undesirable feature splitting and that this framework naturally suggests new hierarchical SAE architectures which provide more concise explanations.

papers.title: A is for Absorption: Studying Feature Splitting and Absorption in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What causes Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to fail in recovering true underlying features when the features form a hierarchy? The paper identifies and studies the phenomenon of feature absorption.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and analyzes the phenomenon of feature absorption in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), showing it is caused by hierarchical features and the sparsity penalty, and introduces a metric to detect it.
papers.conclusion: Feature absorption poses an obstacle to the practical application of SAEs for interpretability, and fundamental theoretical issues need to be addressed before SAEs can be used robustly at scale.
papers.key_findings:
Feature absorption occurs in SAEs when features form a hierarchy, causing seemingly monosemantic latents to fail to fire where they should.
The phenomenon is caused by the sparsity penalty in SAEs.
The paper proposes a metric to detect feature absorption and validates it on hundreds of LLM SAEs.
Feature absorption is widespread and occurs in every LLM SAE tested.
Varying SAE sizes or sparsity is insufficient to solve the issue.
papers.limitation:
The absorption metric is limited to early layers (before layer 18 in Gemma 2 2B) because attention moves information to later tokens, making causal interventions ineffective at later layers.
The absorption metric is likely an underestimate of true absorption because it only captures cases where a single latent dominates and the main latents are fully turned off.
future_direction: Develop improved metrics for feature absorption that can be applied at all model layers and capture partial absorption.
Address the fundamental theoretical issues causing feature absorption to enable robust use of SAEs for interpretability.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) aim to decompose the activation space of large language models (LLMs) into human-interpretable latent directions or features. As we increase the number of features in the SAE, hierarchical features tend to split into finer features ("math" may split into "algebra", "geometry", etc.), a phenomenon referred to as feature splitting. However, we show that sparse decomposition and splitting of hierarchical features is not robust. Specifically, we show that seemingly monosemantic features fail to fire where they should, and instead get "absorbed" into their children features. We coin this phenomenon feature absorption, and show that it is caused by optimizing for sparsity in SAEs whenever the underlying features form a hierarchy. We introduce a metric to detect absorption in SAEs, and validate our findings empirically on hundreds of LLM SAEs. Our investigation suggests that varying SAE sizes or sparsity is insufficient to solve this issue. We discuss the implications of feature absorption in SAEs and some potential approaches to solve the fundamental theoretical issues before SAEs can be used for interpreting LLMs robustly and at scale.

papers.title: Quantifying Feature Space Universality Across Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What is the extent of feature space universality across large language models? Specifically, whether SAE feature spaces are similar under rotation-invariant transformations.
papers.core_contribution: Provides empirical evidence that SAE feature spaces are similar across different LLMs, supporting the Analogous Feature Universality hypothesis, which enables the transfer of interpretability techniques.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that feature spaces are universal across LLMs, providing evidence for the Analogous Feature Universality hypothesis, which can facilitate the transfer of interpretability techniques like steering vectors.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers of LLMs show the highest similarity in SAE feature spaces, while layer 0 has low similarity.
Semantically meaningful subspaces, such as those for emotions or time, exhibit notable similarity across models.
The similarity is statistically significant as measured by SVCCA and RSA, with p-values below 0.05 for most layer pairs.
The approach works across various model pairs, including Pythia, Gemma, and Llama models.
Filtering non-concept features and many-to-1 mappings improves similarity scores.
papers.abstract: The Universality Hypothesis in large language models (LLMs) claims that different models converge towards similar concept representations in their latent spaces. Providing evidence for this hypothesis would enable researchers to exploit universal properties, facilitating the generalization of mechanistic interpretability techniques across models. Previous works studied if LLMs learned the same features, which are internal representations that activate on specific concepts. Since comparing features across LLMs is challenging due to polysemanticity, in which LLM neurons often correspond to multiple unrelated features rather than to distinct concepts, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have been employed to disentangle LLM neurons into SAE features corresponding to distinct concepts. In this paper, we introduce a new variation of the universality hypothesis called Analogous Feature Universality: we hypothesize that even if SAEs across different models learn different feature representations, the spaces spanned by SAE features are similar, such that one SAE space is similar to another SAE space under rotation-invariant transformations. Evidence for this hypothesis would imply that interpretability techniques related to latent spaces, such as steering vectors, may be transferred across models via certain transformations. To investigate this hypothesis, we first pair SAE features across different models via activation correlation, and then measure spatial relation similarities between paired features via representational similarity measures, which transform spaces into representations that reveal hidden relational similarities. Our experiments demonstrate high similarities for SAE feature spaces across various LLMs, providing evidence for feature space universality.

papers.title: From Atoms to Trees: Building a Structured Feature Forest with Hierarchical Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How to capture the hierarchical structure of features in LLM representations, moving beyond isolated feature extraction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Hierarchical Sparse Autoencoder (HSAE), a method that jointly learns sparse autoencoders and parent-child relationships to extract hierarchical feature structures from LLM representations.
papers.conclusion: HSAE is a novel framework that learns conceptual hierarchies from LLM activations, outperforming post-hoc methods and preserving SAE feature quality.
papers.key_findings:
HSAE recovers semantically meaningful hierarchies from LLM activations, as shown by qualitative case studies and quantitative metrics.
HSAE significantly outperforms post-hoc alignment baselines in hierarchical consistency (e.g., lower Hamming distance, higher co-activation probabilities).
HSAE maintains feature quality and reconstruction fidelity comparable to standard SAEs across various dictionary sizes.
The learned hierarchies manifest geometrically: activations triggering sibling features cluster together in the activation space.
Features with multiple children exhibit higher interpretability (AutoInterp scores) than those with a single child.
papers.limitation:
The tree structure is constrained by a fixed number of levels, which may not fully capture varying depths of semantic abstraction.
Some misalignments in parent-child co-activation persist, and it is unclear if they are due to methodological constraints or inherently non-hierarchical activations.
future_direction: Investigate more flexible architectural priors and scaling laws of hierarchical discovery.
Apply hierarchies for multi-scale model steering and safety auditing.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have proven effective for extracting monosemantic features from large language models (LLMs), yet these features are typically identified in isolation. However, broad evidence suggests that LLMs capture the intrinsic structure of natural language, where the phenomenon of "feature splitting" in particular indicates that such structure is hierarchical. To capture this, we propose the Hierarchical Sparse Autoencoder (HSAE), which jointly learns a series of SAEs and the parent-child relationships between their features. HSAE strengthens the alignment between parent and child features through two novel mechanisms: a structural constraint loss and a random feature perturbation mechanism. Extensive experiments across various LLMs and layers demonstrate that HSAE consistently recovers semantically meaningful hierarchies, supported by both qualitative case studies and rigorous quantitative metrics. At the same time, HSAE preserves the reconstruction fidelity and interpretability of standard SAEs across different dictionary sizes. Our work provides a powerful, scalable tool for discovering and analyzing the multi-scale conceptual structures embedded in LLM representations.

papers.title: Evaluating Synthetic Activations composed of SAE Latents in GPT-2
papers.research_question: Do synthetic activations composed of SAE latents behave like real (model-generated) activations in terms of directional sensitivity and activation plateaus? What properties of SAE latents are important for this?
papers.core_contribution: Synthetic activations composed of SAE latents can approximate real activations in directional sensitivity when controlling for sparsity and cosine similarity, but they fail to reproduce activation plateaus, indicating that real activations have additional structure beyond a simple bag of latents.
papers.conclusion: Model-generated activations cannot be explained by simple 'bags of SAE latents'; leveraging statistical and geometric properties of SAE latents helps create synthetic activations more similar to real ones in sensitivity, but these synthetic activations lack the characteristic activation plateaus, suggesting additional latent properties influence model computation.
papers.key_findings:
The 'bag of SAE latents' approach is insufficient to produce synthetic activations that resemble real activations.
Sparsity of the top SAE latent, relative latent activations, and cosine similarity between active latents and the top latent are important for synthetic activations to behave like real activations in sensitivity experiments.
Synthetic activations do not exhibit activation plateaus like real activations do.
SAE reconstructions of real activations behave similarly to real activations, indicating that SAE reconstruction error is not the main cause of the discrepancy.
The model is more sensitive to perturbations towards real activations than random directions, and synthetic-structured activations are more similar to real activations than synthetic-baseline activations in sensitivity experiments.
papers.limitation:
The heuristics for constructing synthetic activations leave room for improvement, as evidenced by the gap between them and model-generated activations, especially for activation plateaus.
The method uses cosine similarity between SAE latents to capture geometric relationships but does not account for latent co-occurrence and other relationships.
The synthetic activations do not match the cosine similarity distribution of SAE latents in model-generated activations closely.
The method leverages information from the base activation to construct synthetic activations (though verified that using a different activation does not change results).
The L2 distance curves exhibit significant variability, impacting the effectiveness of the maximum slope metric; more robust metrics could produce clearer results.
The study focuses solely on one layer of GPT2-small and perturbations confined to the final token position; generalizability to other layers, models, SAEs, and context lengths is not established.
future_direction: Developing better approaches to constructing synthetic activations that perform better in both experimental settings.
Checking for the existence of thresholds below which the model output does not respond to changes in latent activations.
Case studies looking at model sensitivity to perturbations in directions created using interpretable SAE latents and taking context into account.
papers.abstract: Sparse Auto-Encoders (SAEs) are commonly employed in mechanistic interpretability to decompose the residual stream into monosemantic SAE latents. Recent work demonstrates that perturbing a model's activations at an early layer results in a step-function-like change in the model's final layer activations. Furthermore, the model's sensitivity to this perturbation differs between model-generated (real) activations and random activations. In our study, we assess model sensitivity in order to compare real activations to synthetic activations composed of SAE latents. Our findings indicate that synthetic activations closely resemble real activations when we control for the sparsity and cosine similarity of the constituent SAE latents. This suggests that real activations cannot be explained by a simple "bag of SAE latents" lacking internal structure, and instead suggests that SAE latents possess significant geometric and statistical properties. Notably, we observe that our synthetic activations exhibit less pronounced activation plateaus compared to those typically surrounding real activations.

papers.title: Dense SAE Latents Are Features, Not Bugs
papers.research_question: Are dense latents in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) undesirable training artifacts or do they reflect meaningful model representations?
papers.core_contribution: Dense SAE latents are not training artifacts but reflect meaningful, functional representations in the language model's residual stream, serving roles such as position tracking, context binding, and entropy regulation.
papers.conclusion: Dense SAE latents serve functional roles in language model computation and should not be dismissed as training noise.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating the dense-latent subspace in the residual stream prevents new dense latents from being learned in retrained SAEs, indicating dense features are intrinsic to the residual space.
Dense latents tend to form antipodal pairs that reconstruct specific directions in the residual stream.
A taxonomy of dense latents identifies classes including position tracking, context binding, entropy regulation, alphabet (letter-specific output), part-of-speech, and PCA reconstruction.
The function of dense latents shifts across layers: from structural (e.g., position) in early layers, to semantic (e.g., context binding) in middle layers, to output-oriented (e.g., alphabet) in late layers.
Nullspace-aligned dense latents are causally involved in entropy regulation via interaction with RMSNorm scaling.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to a few models (Gemma 2 2B, GPT-2, LLaMA 3.2) and SAE architectures (JumpReLU, TopK).
future_direction: Explore the circuits involving dense subspaces, particularly context-binding latents.
Investigate whether dense latents are a general phenomenon across more models and SAE variants.
Challenge the assumption of globally monosemantic directions and further study context-dependent feature binding.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are designed to extract interpretable features from language models by enforcing a sparsity constraint. Ideally, training an SAE would yield latents that are both sparse and semantically meaningful. However, many SAE latents activate frequently (i.e., are \emph{dense}), raising concerns that they may be undesirable artifacts of the training procedure. In this work, we systematically investigate the geometry, function, and origin of dense latents and show that they are not only persistent but often reflect meaningful model representations. We first demonstrate that dense latents tend to form antipodal pairs that reconstruct specific directions in the residual stream, and that ablating their subspace suppresses the emergence of new dense features in retrained SAEs -- suggesting that high density features are an intrinsic property of the residual space. We then introduce a taxonomy of dense latents, identifying classes tied to position tracking, context binding, entropy regulation, letter-specific output signals, part-of-speech, and principal component reconstruction. Finally, we analyze how these features evolve across layers, revealing a shift from structural features in early layers, to semantic features in mid layers, and finally to output-oriented signals in the last layers of the model. Our findings indicate that dense latents serve functional roles in language model computation and should not be dismissed as training noise.

papers.title: Automatically Interpreting Millions of Features in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to automatically generate and evaluate natural language interpretations for millions of features in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) applied to large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an automated pipeline and five new scoring techniques (detection, fuzzing, surprisal, embedding, intervention) for generating and evaluating natural language interpretations of SAE features, which are more efficient than existing methods.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents an automated pipeline for interpreting SAE features, introduces efficient scoring methods, and shows that intervention scoring can explain features not captured by correlational methods.
papers.key_findings:
New scoring methods (detection, fuzzing, surprisal, embedding, intervention) are more compute-efficient than simulation scoring and correlate with human judgments.
Intervention scoring provides causal explanations for features that are poorly explained by correlational methods.
Sampling activating contexts from the entire activation distribution improves interpretation quality compared to only top activations.
Larger explainer models produce better interpretations, but benefits saturate beyond a certain size.
SAE features are more interpretable than the original model's neurons.
papers.limitation:
The pipeline does not handle long-range features that activate over longer contexts.
Intervention scoring requires careful control of intervention strength to avoid trivial interpretability.
Existing scoring techniques have pitfalls, such as simulation scoring ignoring non-activating contexts.
future_direction: Explanation of long-range features that activate over longer contexts.
papers.abstract: While the activations of neurons in deep neural networks usually do not have a simple human-understandable interpretation, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can be used to transform these activations into a higher-dimensional latent space which may be more easily interpretable. However, these SAEs can have millions of distinct latent features, making it infeasible for humans to manually interpret each one. In this work, we build an open-source automated pipeline to generate and evaluate natural language explanations for SAE features using LLMs. We test our framework on SAEs of varying sizes, activation functions, and losses, trained on two different open-weight LLMs. We introduce five new techniques to score the quality of explanations that are cheaper to run than the previous state of the art. One of these techniques, intervention scoring, evaluates the interpretability of the effects of intervening on a feature, which we find explains features that are not recalled by existing methods. We propose guidelines for generating better explanations that remain valid for a broader set of activating contexts, and discuss pitfalls with existing scoring techniques. We use our explanations to measure the semantic similarity of independently trained SAEs, and find that SAEs trained on nearby layers of the residual stream are highly similar. Our large-scale analysis confirms that SAE latents are indeed much more interpretable than neurons, even when neurons are sparsified using top-$k$ postprocessing. Our code is available at https://github.com/EleutherAI/sae-auto-interp, and our explanations are available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/EleutherAI/auto_interp_explanations.

papers.title: Attribution-Guided Distillation of Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we distill a compact, reusable core of consistently useful features from Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders to improve feature consistency and transferability across training runs and sparsity levels?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DMSAEs, an attribution-guided training pipeline that distills a compact, reusable core of latent features from Matryoshka SAEs, improving feature consistency and transferability across sparsity levels.
papers.conclusion: DMSAEs provide a practical route toward feature consistency across SAEs and transferability of interpretations across training runs and sparsity levels.
papers.key_findings:
Seven cycles of distillation on Gemma-2-2B layer 12 activations yielded a distilled core of 197 features that were repeatedly selected.
Training SAEs using the distilled core improves several SAEBench metrics, including absorption and RAVEL, compared to Matryoshka SAE baselines.
The method demonstrates that consistent sets of latent features can be transferred across sparsity levels.
Attribution-guided distillation identifies core latents that remain systematically useful for reconstruction, unlike a randomly initialized core which is driven towards zero activity.
papers.limitation:
Requires multiple cycles of distillation, leading to much higher computational costs relative to training a single Matryoshka SAE.
Core selection depends on the gradient × activation attribution method, which is a fast first-order approximation but may be suboptimal.
Freezing encoder weight vectors stabilizes detection directions, but encoder biases and decoder weights are reinitialized, so latent behavior (threshold, firing rate, contribution) can still change across cycles.
future_direction: Reducing the computational cost of distillation.
Extending the DMSAE framework to other models and scientific domains.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) aim to disentangle model activations into monosemantic, human-interpretable features. In practice, learned features are often redundant and vary across training runs and sparsity levels, which makes interpretations difficult to transfer and reuse. We introduce Distilled Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders (DMSAEs), a training pipeline that distills a compact core of consistently useful features and reuses it to train new SAEs. DMSAEs run an iterative distillation cycle: train a Matryoshka SAE with a shared core, use gradient X activation to measure each feature's contribution to next-token loss in the most nested reconstruction, and keep only the smallest subset that explains a fixed fraction of the attribution. Only the core encoder weight vectors are transferred across cycles; the core decoder and all non-core latents are reinitialized each time. On Gemma-2-2B layer 12 residual stream activations, seven cycles of distillation (500M tokens, 65k width) yielded a distilled core of 197 features that were repeatedly selected. Training using this distilled core improves several SAEBench metrics and demonstrates that consistent sets of latent features can be transferred across sparsity levels

papers.title: Autoencoders Learn Generative Linear Models
papers.research_question: Under what conditions can shallow two-layer autoencoders trained with gradient descent recover the parameters of underlying generative linear models (e.g., mixture of Gaussians, sparse coding)?
papers.core_contribution: Proves that under suitable conditions, shallow two-layer autoencoders trained with gradient descent can provably recover the parameters of several generative linear models.
papers.conclusion: The work provides theoretical evidence that shallow autoencoders can be used as feature learning mechanisms for a variety of data models, and may offer insight for training deeper stacked architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Autoencoders can learn the parameters of mixture-of-Gaussians, sparse coding, and non-negative sparse coding models under appropriate initialization and hyperparameters.
The code consistency property (recovering the support/sign of the latent code) is crucial for establishing convergence.
The choice of activation function (ReLU or hard thresholding) and bias affects the dynamics and convergence guarantees.
Gradient descent with column-wise normalization exhibits linear convergence to a neighborhood of the ground truth parameters.
The analysis provides theoretical evidence for autoencoders as feature learning mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical analysis requires specific conditions (e.g., incoherence, sparsity, initialization close to ground truth) and does not account for optimization from random initialization far from the ground truth.
Experiments are limited to synthetic data and the theory does not cover finite sample complexity.
future_direction: Finite sample complexity analysis.
Extension to more general architectures.
Extension to richer classes of generative models.
papers.abstract: We provide a series of results for unsupervised learning with autoencoders. Specifically, we study shallow two-layer autoencoder architectures with shared weights. We focus on three generative models for data that are common in statistical machine learning: (i) the mixture-of-gaussians model, (ii) the sparse coding model, and (iii) the sparsity model with non-negative coefficients. For each of these models, we prove that under suitable choices of hyperparameters, architectures, and initialization, autoencoders learned by gradient descent can successfully recover the parameters of the corresponding model. To our knowledge, this is the first result that rigorously studies the dynamics of gradient descent for weight-sharing autoencoders. Our analysis can be viewed as theoretical evidence that shallow autoencoder modules indeed can be used as feature learning mechanisms for a variety of data models, and may shed insight on how to train larger stacked architectures with autoencoders as basic building blocks.

papers.title: Warp: a method for neural network interpretability applied to gene expression profiles
papers.research_question: How can neural networks be interpreted in the context of gene expression analysis to recover meaningful information on a sample-specific basis?
papers.core_contribution: Warping is a method for neural network interpretability that recovers sample-specific gene signatures by interpolating in input or representation space, demonstrating effectiveness on linearly and non-linearly separable datasets.
papers.conclusion: Warping shows promise as a flexible method for post-hoc interpretation of neural networks in computational biology, enabling the examination of class gene signatures with sample-specific insights.
papers.key_findings:
Warping works well on non-linearly separable datasets like XOR, allowing data points to migrate across decision boundaries.
The method provides sample-specific bias vectors, highlighting individual adjustments needed for classification changes.
In a VAE-based approach, warping recovers biologically meaningful gene expression adjustments, such as suppressing surfactant genes and boosting kidney-specific genes to change phenotype classification.
papers.limitation:
Linear interpolation assumes the data manifold is continuous in input space, which may lead to adversarial examples.
Reconstruction blurriness caused by the variational autoencoder encoding.
future_direction: Determine how destructive warps are to other gene signatures within samples.
Overcome reconstruction blurriness caused by the VAE encoding.
papers.abstract: We show a proof of principle for warping, a method to interpret the inner working of neural networks in the context of gene expression analysis. Warping is an efficient way to gain insight to the inner workings of neural nets and make them more interpretable. We demonstrate the ability of warping to recover meaningful information for a given class on a samplespecific individual basis. We found warping works well in both linearly and nonlinearly separable datasets. These encouraging results show that warping has a potential to be the answer to neural networks interpretability in computational biology.

papers.title: Unveiling Decision-Making in LLMs for Text Classification : Extraction of influential and interpretable concepts with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How effective are Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) based explainability approaches for sentence classification, and can a novel supervised SAE variant (ClassifSAE) improve the causality and interpretability of extracted concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ClassifSAE, a supervised Sparse Autoencoder variant for text classification that extracts more interpretable and causal concepts from LLMs, and proposes two new metrics (ConceptSim and SentenceSim) for evaluating concept precision.
papers.conclusion: ClassifSAE is an effective method for extracting interpretable and causal concepts from LLMs for text classification, offering a good trade-off between interpretability and causality.
papers.key_findings:
ClassifSAE produces concepts with higher interpretability (ConceptSim) and better sparsity than baselines.
ClassifSAE achieves second-best causality scores (after HI-Concept) but with better interpretability.
ClassifSAE is computationally more efficient, requiring up to 83% less training time than HI-Concept.
The joint classifier and activation rate sparsity loss in ClassifSAE improve disentanglement and sparsity of concepts.
ClassifSAE can identify fine-grained concepts beyond coarse label categories.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have been successfully used to probe Large Language Models (LLMs) and extract interpretable concepts from their internal representations. These concepts are linear combinations of neuron activations that correspond to human-interpretable features. In this paper, we investigate the effectiveness of SAE-based explainability approaches for sentence classification, a domain where such methods have not been extensively explored. We present a novel SAE-based model ClassifSAE tailored for text classification, leveraging a specialized classifier head and incorporating an activation rate sparsity loss. We benchmark this architecture against established methods such as ConceptShap, Independent Component Analysis, HI-Concept and a standard TopK-SAE baseline. Our evaluation covers several classification benchmarks and backbone LLMs. We further enrich our analysis with two novel metrics for measuring the precision of concept-based explanations, using an external sentence encoder. Our empirical results show that ClassifSAE improves both the causality and interpretability of the extracted features.

papers.title: Empirical Evaluation of Progressive Coding for Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently obtain high-fidelity, interpretable SAEs of different sizes for LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces and compares two methods for progressive coding in sparse autoencoders (Matryoshka SAEs and a permutation/pruning method), demonstrating a trade-off between reconstruction fidelity and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The paper discusses the trade-off between reconstruction fidelity and interpretability in progressive SAE methods, suggesting that Matryoshka SAEs offer better performance while pruned SAEs offer better interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Dictionary importance in vanilla SAEs follows a power law.
Matryoshka SAEs exhibit lower reconstruction loss and higher representational similarity compared to baseline SAEs.
Pruned vanilla SAEs (via permutation) are more interpretable than Matryoshka SAEs.
Both methods allow efficient progressive coding, with Matryoshka SAEs performing better on reconstruction fidelity.
Feature splitting occurs as SAE size increases, affecting performance when using only a subset of features.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on relatively modest-sized SAEs compared to recent work, and methods remain to be validated at larger scales.
Decoder kernel implementation leads to redundant computations in Matryoshka SAEs.
Feature-splitting presents a limitation when distilling large SAEs into smaller ones via permutation, as selecting only the most important split features fails to capture complete functionality.
future_direction: Validating methods at larger scales.
Improving decoder kernel implementation to avoid redundant computations.
Developing methods to recombine or reverse feature-splitting during distillation.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) \citep{bricken2023monosemanticity,gao2024scalingevaluatingsparseautoencoders} rely on dictionary learning to extract interpretable features from neural networks at scale in an unsupervised manner, with applications to representation engineering and information retrieval. SAEs are, however, computationally expensive \citep{lieberum2024gemmascopeopensparse}, especially when multiple SAEs of different sizes are needed. We show that dictionary importance in vanilla SAEs follows a power law. We compare progressive coding based on subset pruning of SAEs -- to jointly training nested SAEs, or so-called {\em Matryoshka} SAEs \citep{bussmann2024learning,nabeshima2024Matryoshka} -- on a language modeling task. We show Matryoshka SAEs exhibit lower reconstruction loss and recaptured language modeling loss, as well as higher representational similarity. Pruned vanilla SAEs are more interpretable, however. We discuss the origins and implications of this trade-off.

papers.title: Interpretable and Testable Vision Features via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we understand vision models by not only interpreting their learned features but also validating these interpretations through controlled experiments?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide a practical, post-hoc method that bridges the gap between concept discovery and causal probing in vision models, enabling both interpretation and controlled testing of learned features.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders enable both hypothesis formation and controlled testing for vision models, providing a foundation for empirically validated model interpretation that unites explanation with experimentation.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on vision transformer activations discover interpretable, monosemantic features corresponding to visual concepts (e.g., cultural symbols, abstract concepts like 'accidents').
CLIP, trained with language supervision, learns abstract semantic features (e.g., country-specific patterns, style-agnostic concepts) that DINOv2, trained with purely visual objectives, does not reliably capture.
SAE-derived features enable precise causal interventions: suppressing a 'blue feathers' feature in a bird image shifts the classification prediction to a similar bird without blue plumage.
SAE features behave as a pseudo-orthogonal basis; suppressing a concept like 'sand' in semantic segmentation affects only the targeted regions without meaningfully altering other predictions.
The method supports patch-level causal edits across different tasks (classification and segmentation) without retraining the original vision transformer or task heads.
papers.limitation:
Discovering interesting SAE units depends on manual browsing of exemplar grids, which is slow, may overlook concepts, and risks cherry-picking.
The work relies on qualitative evaluation through visual inspection, lacking standardized quantitative metrics for measuring interpretability and control effectiveness.
Large interventions on SAE features can push activations off-manifold, and feature correlations/complex interactions complicate clean causal attribution.
SAEs are not guaranteed to surface every concept a model encodes, and low-activation units can be polysemantic or vary across random initializations.
Validation is limited to fine-grained classification and semantic segmentation; broader task coverage and comparison to prior editable concept frameworks (e.g., DN-CBM) are needed.
future_direction: Automating feature discovery and concept-label assignment (e.g., via language supervision).
Developing robust quantitative metrics for semantic alignment, manipulation specificity, and cross-model comparability.
Extending reliable feature control to more sophisticated visual reasoning tasks and understanding feature interactions across different model architectures.
papers.abstract: To truly understand vision models, we must not only interpret their learned features but also validate these interpretations through controlled experiments. While earlier work offers either rich semantics or direct control, few post-hoc tools supply both in a single, model-agnostic procedure. We use sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to bridge this gap; each sparse feature comes with real-image exemplars that reveal its meaning and a decoding vector that can be manipulated to probe its influence on downstream task behavior. By applying our method to widely-used pre-trained vision models, we reveal meaningful differences in the semantic abstractions learned by different pre-training objectives. We then show that a single SAE trained on frozen ViT activations supports patch-level causal edits across tasks (classification and segmentation) all without retraining the ViT or task heads. These qualitative, falsifiable demonstrations position SAEs as a practical bridge between concept discovery and causal probing of vision models. We provide code, demos and models on our project website: https://osu-nlp-group.github.io/saev.

papers.title: Visual Exploration of Feature Relationships in Sparse Autoencoders with Curated Concepts
papers.research_question: How can we enable effective, focused exploration of the relationships between sparse autoencoder (SAE) features and human-interpretable concepts in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a focused exploration framework and an interactive visualization system (SAE Semantic Explorer) that integrates topology-based visual encodings with dimensionality reduction to enable targeted analysis of relationships between SAE features and curated concepts.
papers.conclusion: The proposed visualization framework provides a scalable and interpretable means of exploring how user-defined concepts relate to the structured knowledge encoded in SAEs across layers, facilitating deeper insight into model organization.
papers.key_findings:
The framework reveals that concept relationships evolve across model layers, with early layers showing dense clustering, middle layers showing separation and specialization, and deeper layers showing more integrated structures.
The ball mapper view provides a complementary perspective to UMAP, preserving local neighborhood relationships and revealing structural distortions introduced by dimensionality reduction.
The tool enables the discovery of semantic boundaries and transitions between related concepts, such as tracing a path from 'Computer Science' to 'Mathematics' in the feature space.
papers.limitation: The reliability of identified features depends heavily on the quality of their automatically generated explanations (auto-interpretability).
future_direction: Enhance the UMAP visualization by integrating scalable and annotated visualization toolkits.
Leverage LLMs to automatically generate richer, context-aware explanations for mapper nodes.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful tool for uncovering interpretable features in large language models (LLMs) through the sparse directions they learn. However, the sheer number of extracted directions makes comprehensive exploration intractable. While conventional embedding techniques such as UMAP can reveal global structure, they suffer from limitations including high-dimensional compression artifacts, overplotting, and misleading neighborhood distortions. In this work, we propose a focused exploration framework that prioritizes curated concepts and their corresponding SAE features over attempts to visualize all available features simultaneously. We present an interactive visualization system that combines topology-based visual encoding with dimensionality reduction to faithfully represent both local and global relationships among selected features. This hybrid approach enables users to investigate SAE behavior through targeted, interpretable subsets, facilitating deeper and more nuanced analysis of concept representation in latent space.

papers.title: From superposition to sparse codes: interpretable representations in neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we relate distributed neural representations back to human-interpretable concepts?
papers.core_contribution: This perspective paper presents a theoretical framework explaining how neural networks encode information in superposition and argues that sparse coding, supported by identifiability theory and compressed sensing, can extract interpretable, sparse features from these distributed representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that neural networks learn linear representations of latent variables and that sparse coding can recover interpretable features, providing a foundation for understanding neural representations in both artificial and biological systems.
papers.key_findings:
