If L0 is too low, the SAE will mix correlated features to improve reconstruction. If L0 is too high, the SAE finds degenerate solutions that also mix features. Further, we present a proxy metric that can help guide the search for the correct L0 for an SAE on a given training distribution. We show that our method finds the correct L0 in toy models and coincides with peak sparse probing performance in LLM SAEs. We find that most commonly used SAEs have an L0 that is too low. Our work shows that L0 must be set correctly to train SAEs with correct features.

papers.title: CytoSAE: Interpretable Cell Embeddings for Hematology
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be applied for interpretable morphological concept discovery in hematological imaging?
papers.core_contribution: CytoSAE is a sparse autoencoder that discovers interpretable morphological concepts in hematological images, generalizes across diverse and out-of-domain datasets, and enables explainable disease classification at patch, image, patient, and disease levels.
papers.conclusion: CytoSAE successfully learns interpretable morphological features across different hematological datasets, maintains generalizability to out-of-domain data, and enables multi-level analysis for interpretable disease classification.
papers.key_findings:
CytoSAE discovers morphologically relevant concepts that generalize across peripheral blood and bone marrow cytology datasets, validated by medical experts.
Patch-wise attribution allows sub-cellular level analysis of concepts, highlighting consistent morphological features across datasets.
Patient-level concept barcodes reveal disease-specific morphological features for AML subtypes, such as monocytic precursors for CBFB::MYH11 and granulated blasts for PML::RARA.
CytoSAE concepts achieve multi-class classification performance comparable to state-of-the-art deep learning methods while providing explainability.
Ablation studies show the number of discovered concepts is stable across expansion factors and hyperparameters, with optimal layers between 7–11 for concept balance.
papers.limitation: Manual expert validation was conducted only at the dataset level, not per patient, to avoid human selection bias in concept discovery.
future_direction: Explore patient-specific concept retrieval while minimizing subjectivity.
Incorporate semi-supervised learning techniques to refine the discovered features further.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) emerged as a promising tool for mechanistic interpretability of transformer-based foundation models. Very recently, SAEs were also adopted for the visual domain, enabling the discovery of visual concepts and their patch-wise attribution to tokens in the transformer model. While a growing number of foundation models emerged for medical imaging, tools for explaining their inferences are still lacking. In this work, we show the applicability of SAEs for hematology. We propose CytoSAE, a sparse autoencoder which is trained on over 40,000 peripheral blood single-cell images. CytoSAE generalizes to diverse and out-of-domain datasets, including bone marrow cytology, where it identifies morphologically relevant concepts which we validated with medical experts. Furthermore, we demonstrate scenarios in which CytoSAE can generate patient-specific and disease-specific concepts, enabling the detection of pathognomonic cells and localized cellular abnormalities at the patch level. We quantified the effect of concepts on a patient-level AML subtype classification task and show that CytoSAE concepts reach performance comparable to the state-of-the-art, while offering explainability on the sub-cellular level. Source code and model weights are available at https://github.com/dynamical-inference/cytosae.

papers.title: Applying sparse autoencoders to unlearn knowledge in language models
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can be used to remove knowledge from language models in an interpretable way.
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that individual interpretable SAE features can be used to unlearn knowledge from language models, but current SAE quality or intervention techniques result in similar or larger side-effects than fine-tuning based methods like Representation Misdirection for Unlearning (RMU).
papers.conclusion: SAE-based unlearning is possible but currently has limitations; improvements in SAE quality or intervention techniques are needed to make it comparable to fine-tuning based techniques.
papers.key_findings:
Individual SAE features can be used to unlearn knowledge from language models.
Negative scaling of feature activations is necessary for unlearning; zero ablating features is ineffective.
Intervening on multiple SAE features simultaneously can unlearn multiple topics, but with similar or larger unwanted side-effects than the existing RMU technique.
The specific decoder vectors are important for unlearning in gemma-2-2b-it, but not as critical in gemma-2b-it.
The SAE-based unlearning method only modifies the model's activations, not the weights, so the original knowledge remains in the weights.
papers.limitation:
The SAE-based unlearning method only modifies the model's activations, without modifying the model weights, so the original knowledge is still contained in the weights.
Current SAE quality or intervention techniques would need to improve to make SAE-based unlearning comparable to the existing fine-tuning based techniques.
SAE-based unlearning results in similar or larger unwanted side-effects than the existing RMU technique.
future_direction: Examine how SAE quality and width impact unlearning effectiveness.
Compare SAE-based unlearning to activation steering using bio-related and non-bio-related prompt pairs.
Investigate how SAE interventions affect related features in subsequent layers to better understand the unlearning mechanism.
papers.abstract: We investigate whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can be used to remove knowledge from language models. We use the biology subset of the Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy dataset and test on the gemma-2b-it and gemma-2-2b-it language models. We demonstrate that individual interpretable biology-related SAE features can be used to unlearn a subset of WMDP-Bio questions with minimal side-effects in domains other than biology. Our results suggest that negative scaling of feature activations is necessary and that zero ablating features is ineffective. We find that intervening using multiple SAE features simultaneously can unlearn multiple different topics, but with similar or larger unwanted side-effects than the existing Representation Misdirection for Unlearning technique. Current SAE quality or intervention techniques would need to improve to make SAE-based unlearning comparable to the existing fine-tuning based techniques.

papers.title: The cell as a token: high-dimensional geometry in language models and cell embeddings
papers.research_question: How can advances in understanding the geometry of language model embeddings inform the analysis of single-cell genomics data?
papers.core_contribution: This review highlights how principles from language model embeddings, such as context-dependence and low-dimensional manifolds, can guide the development and interpretation of single-cell foundation models.
papers.conclusion: Drawing parallels between language models and single-cell embeddings reveals shared principles in high-dimensional geometry, but biological context is more complex, requiring future models to integrate multimodal data and address dynamical processes.
papers.key_findings:
The distributional hypothesis in language, which links word meaning to context, can be analogously applied to single-cell data for self-supervised learning of cell embeddings.
Low-dimensional manifolds in embedding spaces capture semantic relationships in language and developmental pathways in biology, enabling analogies and trajectory inference.
Dynamic embeddings that incorporate context, such as through self-attention in language models or spatial data in cells, improve representation fidelity and disambiguation.
Interpretability methods like linear probes and sparse autoencoders, used in language models, can be adapted to analyze internal representations in single-cell foundation models for feature identification.
The analogy between cells and tokens has limitations due to the ordered, discrete nature of language context versus the multiscale, indirect context of biological systems.
papers.limitation: Biological context is multiscale, incomplete, and indirect compared to the discrete, ordered sequences in language, limiting direct analogies.
future_direction: Integrating diverse experimental contexts and multimodal data without loss of biological specificity in cell embeddings.
Developing improved benchmarks to test the ability of foundation models to parse complex and indirect regulatory logic in biology.
Creating temporally aware embedding models that capture continuous trajectories and causal relationships in dynamical biological systems.
papers.abstract: Single-cell sequencing technology maps cells to a high-dimensional space encoding their internal activity. Recently-proposed virtual cell models extend this concept, enriching cells' representations based on patterns learned from pretraining on vast cell atlases. This review explores how advances in understanding the structure of natural language embeddings informs ongoing efforts to analyze single-cell datasets. Both fields process unstructured data by partitioning datasets into tokens embedded within a high-dimensional vector space. We discuss how the context of tokens influences the geometry of embedding space, and how low-dimensional manifolds shape this space's robustness and interpretation. We highlight how new developments in foundation models for language, such as interpretability probes and in-context reasoning, can inform efforts to construct cell atlases and train virtual cell models.

papers.title: Features that Make a Difference: Leveraging Gradients for Improved Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) be improved to learn features that are more causally relevant to model outputs by incorporating gradient information?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Gradient SAEs (g-SAEs), which modify the TopK activation function in sparse autoencoders to incorporate gradient information, resulting in latents that are more causally relevant and better for steering model outputs without sacrificing interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Incorporating gradient information into SAEs improves their ability to capture causally relevant features and enhances steerability without compromising interpretability, advancing dictionary learning towards accounting for both representational and causal aspects of model features.
papers.key_findings:
g-SAEs produce reconstructions that are more faithful to original network performance for a given sparsity level.
g-SAEs learn latents that are more effective at steering models in arbitrary contexts, increasing the probability of associated tokens more strongly and specifically.
g-SAEs have fewer permanently inactive ('dead') latents compared to other SAE architectures.
g-SAEs show improved performance (lower loss added) across different model sizes (GPT-2 small to xl).
g-SAEs do not sacrifice interpretability, as human evaluators rate them similarly to standard TopK SAEs.
papers.limitation:
Activation plateaus: models may be robust to small perturbations, so gradients might not capture sensitivity to larger perturbations.
Computational complexity: g-SAEs require backpropagation, though in practice it was not a bottleneck.
Evaluations: need for more thorough evaluations and understanding of how token-level steerability translates to higher levels of abstraction.
future_direction: Investigating how to incorporate higher-order derivative information to address activation plateaus.
Developing more comprehensive evaluation frameworks for SAEs.
Studying how increased steerability on the token level translates to higher levels of abstraction.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are a promising approach for extracting neural network features by learning a sparse and overcomplete decomposition of the network's internal activations.However, SAEs are traditionally trained considering only activation values and not the effect those activations have on downstream computations.This limits the information available to learn features, and biases the autoencoder towards neglecting features which are represented with small activation values but strongly influence model outputs.To address this, we introduce Gradient SAEs (g-SAEs), which modify the k-sparse autoencoder architecture by augmenting the TopK activation function to rely on the gradients of the input activation when selecting the k elements.For a given sparsity level, g-SAEs produce reconstructions that are more faithful to original network performance when propagated through the network.Additionally, we find evidence that g-SAEs learn latents that are on average more effective at steering models in arbitrary contexts.By considering the downstream effects of activations, our approach leverages the dual nature of neural network features as both representations, retrospectively, and actions, prospectively.While previous methods have approached the problem of feature discovery primarily focused on the former aspect, g-SAEs represent a step towards accounting for the latter as well.

papers.title: Taming Polysemanticity in LLMs: Provable Feature Recovery via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How to formulate a statistical model for feature recovery in polysemantic LLM representations, and design an SAE training algorithm with provable recovery guarantees and practical effectiveness.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a statistical framework for feature recovery in polysemantic LLM representations and proposes Group Bias Adaptation (GBA), an SAE training algorithm with provable recovery guarantees and improved empirical performance.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a statistical framework and the GBA algorithm for provable feature recovery in SAEs, advancing mechanistic interpretability with theoretical guarantees and empirical improvements.
papers.key_findings:
Proposes a statistical model that formalizes polysemantic features as sparse mixtures of underlying monosemantic concepts.
Introduces Group Bias Adaptation (GBA), an SAE training algorithm that uses bias adaptation to control neuron sparsity without hyperparameter tuning.
Provides the first provable recovery guarantee for an SAE algorithm, showing GBA recovers all monosemantic features under the statistical model.
Empirically demonstrates GBA achieves superior sparsity-loss trade-off and feature consistency on LLMs up to 1.5B parameters compared to baseline methods.
future_direction: Extending the statistical framework to more complex data distributions.
Scaling GBA to larger models.
Exploring applications in model steering and control.
papers.abstract: We study the challenge of achieving theoretically grounded feature recovery using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for the interpretation of Large Language Models. Existing SAE training algorithms often lack rigorous mathematical guarantees and suffer from practical limitations such as hyperparameter sensitivity and instability. To address these issues, we first propose a novel statistical framework for the feature recovery problem, which includes a new notion of feature identifiability by modeling polysemantic features as sparse mixtures of underlying monosemantic concepts. Building on this framework, we introduce a new SAE training algorithm based on ``bias adaptation'', a technique that adaptively adjusts neural network bias parameters to ensure appropriate activation sparsity. We theoretically \highlight{prove that this algorithm correctly recovers all monosemantic features} when input data is sampled from our proposed statistical model. Furthermore, we develop an improved empirical variant, Group Bias Adaptation (GBA), and \highlight{demonstrate its superior performance against benchmark methods when applied to LLMs with up to 1.5 billion parameters}. This work represents a foundational step in demystifying SAE training by providing the first SAE algorithm with theoretical recovery guarantees, thereby advancing the development of more transparent and trustworthy AI systems through enhanced mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: DLM-Scope: Mechanistic Interpretability of Diffusion Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) be used for mechanistic interpretability in diffusion language models (DLMs), and how do their properties and applications differ from those in autoregressive LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DLM-Scope, the first SAE-based interpretability framework for Diffusion Language Models (DLMs), demonstrating that SAEs can extract interpretable features, enable effective diffusion-time steering, analyze decoding order, and transfer from base to instruction-tuned models.
papers.conclusion: DLM-Scope establishes a foundation for mechanistic interpretability in DLMs and shows the great potential of applying SAEs to DLM-related tasks and algorithms.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on DLMs achieve a favorable sparsity-fidelity trade-off and can even reduce cross-entropy loss when inserted in early layers, a phenomenon absent or weaker in LLMs.
SAE features enable effective diffusion-time interventions (steering) that often outperform single-pass LLM steering.
SAE feature dynamics provide a useful signal for analyzing and correlating with the performance of different DLM decoding-order strategies.
Base-trained SAEs transfer almost losslessly to instruction-tuned DLMs in shallow and middle layers, but not in the deepest layer, indicating tuning-specific changes in deep representations.
future_direction: As DLMs scale, we plan to extend SAEs to more DLMs to better understand and improve models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a standard tool for mechanistic interpretability in autoregressive large language models (LLMs), enabling researchers to extract sparse, human-interpretable features and intervene on model behavior. Recently, as diffusion language models (DLMs) have become an increasingly promising alternative to the autoregressive LLMs, it is essential to develop tailored mechanistic interpretability tools for this emerging class of models. In this work, we present DLM-Scope, the first SAE-based interpretability framework for DLMs, and demonstrate that trained Top-K SAEs can faithfully extract interpretable features. Notably, we find that inserting SAEs affects DLMs differently than autoregressive LLMs: while SAE insertion in LLMs typically incurs a loss penalty, in DLMs it can reduce cross-entropy loss when applied to early layers, a phenomenon absent or markedly weaker in LLMs. Additionally, SAE features in DLMs enable more effective diffusion-time interventions, often outperforming LLM steering. Moreover, we pioneer certain new SAE-based research directions for DLMs: we show that SAEs can provide useful signals for DLM decoding order; and the SAE features are stable during the post-training phase of DLMs. Our work establishes a foundation for mechanistic interpretability in DLMs and shows a great potential of applying SAEs to DLM-related tasks and algorithms.

papers.title: Evaluating and Designing Sparse Autoencoders by Approximating Quasi-Orthogonality
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) be evaluated and designed with a theoretical grounding for sparsity, avoiding the need to manually tune the hyperparameter k?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Approximate Feature Activation (AFA), a theoretical framework linking input embedding norms to sparse feature activation norms, and top-AFA, an activation function that adaptively selects the number of active features per input without tuning k.
papers.conclusion: The AFA framework addresses a core limitation in SAE design by providing a principled way to link input embeddings to feature activations, and top-AFA SAE demonstrates improved performance over fixed-sparsity methods.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed top-AFA SAE outperforms top-k and batch top-k SAEs in reconstruction performance on GPT-2 layers.
The εLBO metric provides a different evaluation perspective on SAE quality compared to mean squared error (MSE).
The AFA formulation provides a closed-form estimate of the ℓ2-norm of sparse activations with provable error bounds.
Pre-trained SAE decoders often fail to achieve the level of quasi-orthogonality permitted by the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma.
Top-AFA allows adaptive per-input sparsity, removing the need for a fixed sparsity hyperparameter k.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis is limited to the linear representation hypothesis; extending AFA to more general superposition settings remains an open question.
Top-AFA introduces a new hyperparameter λAFA and can result in high ℓ0 values.
future_direction: Extending AFA to more general superposition settings, such as when Φ(·) is a two-layer neural network or other SAE variants like Matryoshka SAEs.
A deeper investigation into the necessity of the loss coefficient λAFA.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used in mechanistic interpretability research for large language models; however, the state-of-the-art method of using $k$-sparse autoencoders lacks a theoretical grounding for selecting the hyperparameter $k$ that represents the number of nonzero activations, often denoted by $\ell_0$. In this paper, we reveal a theoretical link that the $\ell_2$-norm of the sparse feature vector can be approximated with the $\ell_2$-norm of the dense vector with a closed-form error, which allows sparse autoencoders to be trained without the need to manually determine $\ell_0$. Specifically, we validate two applications of our theoretical findings. First, we introduce a new methodology that can assess the feature activations of pre-trained SAEs by computing the theoretically expected value from the input embedding, which has been overlooked by existing SAE evaluation methods and loss functions. Second, we introduce a novel activation function, top-AFA, which builds upon our formulation of approximate feature activation (AFA). This function enables top-$k$ style activation without requiring a constant hyperparameter $k$ to be tuned, dynamically determining the number of activated features for each input. By training SAEs on three intermediate layers to reconstruct GPT2 hidden embeddings for over 80 million tokens from the OpenWebText dataset, we demonstrate the empirical merits of this approach and compare it with current state-of-the-art $k$-sparse autoencoders. Our code is available at: https://github.com/SewoongLee/top-afa-sae.

papers.title: Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can language models be decomposed into interpretable, monosemantic features using dictionary learning to address polysemanticity and superposition?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable, monosemantic features from language model activations, enabling decomposition into understandable components and facilitating circuit analysis.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning with sparse autoencoders is a promising approach for mechanistic interpretability, successfully decomposing language models into monosemantic features and revealing internal structures like feature clusters and automata-like systems.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders extract relatively monosemantic features that are more interpretable than neurons, with most features being human-understandable.
Features can be used to intervene on and steer transformer generation, such as activating specific features to produce corresponding text like base64 or Arabic script.
Features are universal across different models and autoencoder runs, more similar to each other than to neurons, suggesting they reflect underlying data properties.
Features split into families as autoencoder size increases, providing different resolutions of understanding the same model components.
Despite having only 512 neurons, the MLP layer can represent tens of thousands of features through superposition, as shown by scaling the autoencoder.
papers.abstract: How can language models be decomposed into interpretable, monosemantic features using dictionary learning to address polysemanticity and superposition? Sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable, monosemantic features from language model activations, enabling decomposition into understandable components and facilitating circuit analysis. Dictionary learning with sparse autoencoders is a promising approach for mechanistic interpretability, successfully decomposing language models into monosemantic features and revealing internal structures like feature clusters and automata-like systems.

papers.title: Use Sparse Autoencoders to Discover Unknown Concepts, Not to Act on Known Concepts
papers.research_question: How can we reconcile conflicting narratives about the usefulness of sparse autoencoders (SAEs)? The paper argues that SAEs are less effective for acting on known concepts but powerful for discovering unknown concepts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes a conceptual distinction: SAEs are less effective for acting on known concepts but powerful for discovering unknown concepts. It outlines use cases for SAEs in ML interpretability, fairness, auditing, safety, and social/health sciences.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that successful uses of SAEs involve discovering unknown concepts, and this distinction highlights the potential of SAEs for various research areas.
papers.key_findings:
Negative results on SAEs pertain to tasks that act on known concepts, such as concept detection and model steering, where SAEs underperform simple baselines.
Positive results on SAEs involve discovering unknown concepts, such as in hypothesis generation and explaining language model outputs (biology of LLMs).
SAEs can bridge the prediction-explanation gap by converting black box representations into interpretable natural language concepts.
SAEs are a promising tool for applications in ML interpretability, fairness, auditing, safety, and social/health sciences.
future_direction: Using SAEs for ML fairness, interpretability, explainability, auditing, and safety.
Using SAEs in social and health sciences to discover unknown concepts from text data.
Bridging the prediction-explanation gap with SAEs.
papers.abstract: While sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have generated significant excitement, a series of negative results have added to skepticism about their usefulness. Here, we establish a conceptual distinction that reconciles competing narratives surrounding SAEs. We argue that while SAEs may be less effective for acting on known concepts, SAEs are powerful tools for discovering unknown concepts. This distinction cleanly separates existing negative and positive results, and suggests several classes of SAE applications. Specifically, we outline use cases for SAEs in (i) ML interpretability, explainability, fairness, auditing, and safety, and (ii) social and health sciences.

papers.title: From Flat to Hierarchical: Extracting Sparse Representations with Matching Pursuit
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can capture hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features in neural network representations, and whether a new SAE architecture (MP-SAE) can better capture such structures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MP-SAE, a sparse autoencoder based on matching pursuit, which captures hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features in neural representations, outperforming existing SAEs and revealing cross-modal structure in vision-language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that interpretability methods should be grounded in the phenomenology of representations, and that MP-SAE provides a step in this direction by capturing hierarchical and nonlinear structures.
papers.key_findings:
Existing SAEs struggle to capture conditionally orthogonal (hierarchical) features, while MP-SAE can capture both intra-level and inter-level structure.
MP-SAE recovers more expressive features than standard SAEs across various vision models, achieving higher reconstruction accuracy at comparable sparsity.
MP-SAE enables adaptive sparsity at inference time, allowing monotonic improvement in reconstruction error with each step, unlike fixed-sparsity SAEs.
MP-SAE learns dictionaries with higher global coherence but selects less interfering features at inference, promoting conditional orthogonality.
MP-SAE uncovers multimodal features in vision-language models that are shared across modalities, whereas standard SAEs tend to learn modality-specific features.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to hierarchical and nonlinear structures; other forms of structure (e.g., multi-dimensional features) are not addressed.
MP-SAE's inference requires multiple steps, which may be computationally more expensive than standard SAEs.
future_direction: Extending MP-SAE to capture multi-dimensional features.
Applying MP-SAE to larger-scale language models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Motivated by the hypothesis that neural network representations encode abstract, interpretable features as linearly accessible, approximately orthogonal directions, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a popular tool in interpretability. However, recent work has demonstrated phenomenology of model representations that lies outside the scope of this hypothesis, showing signatures of hierarchical, nonlinear, and multi-dimensional features. This raises the question: do SAEs represent features that possess structure at odds with their motivating hypothesis? If not, does avoiding this mismatch help identify said features and gain further insights into neural network representations? To answer these questions, we take a construction-based approach and re-contextualize the popular matching pursuits (MP) algorithm from sparse coding to design MP-SAE -- an SAE that unrolls its encoder into a sequence of residual-guided steps, allowing it to capture hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features. Comparing this architecture with existing SAEs on a mixture of synthetic and natural data settings, we show: (i) hierarchical concepts induce conditionally orthogonal features, which existing SAEs are unable to faithfully capture, and (ii) the nonlinear encoding step of MP-SAE recovers highly meaningful features, helping us unravel shared structure in the seemingly dichotomous representation spaces of different modalities in a vision-language model, hence demonstrating the assumption that useful features are solely linearly accessible is insufficient. We also show that the sequential encoder principle of MP-SAE affords an additional benefit of adaptive sparsity at inference time, which may be of independent interest. Overall, we argue our results provide credence to the idea that interpretability should begin with the phenomenology of representations, with methods emerging from assumptions that fit it.

papers.title: FaithfulSAE: Towards Capturing Faithful Features with Sparse Autoencoders without External Dataset Dependencies
papers.research_question: How does training Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) on out-of-distribution data affect their stability and feature faithfulness, and can training on the model's own synthetic data improve these aspects?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes FaithfulSAE, a method to train Sparse Autoencoders on the model's own synthetic data, which improves feature stability and reduces fake features compared to training on external datasets.
papers.conclusion: Training SAEs on the model's own synthetic data (FaithfulSAE) improves feature consistency and reduces fake features, advancing interpretability by better capturing model-internal features.
papers.key_findings:
FaithfulSAEs trained on synthetic data show higher stability across seeds compared to SAEs trained on instruction datasets.
FaithfulSAEs achieve lower Fake Feature Ratio in 5 out of 7 models compared to web-based dataset trained SAEs.
FaithfulSAEs outperform web-based SAEs in SAE probing tasks, indicating better reconstruction of the model's hidden state.
Shared Feature Ratio is higher when the target model and source model for synthetic data are the same, indicating that SAE training on its own data is more stable.
papers.limitation:
Lack of evaluation on instruction-tuned or reasoning models.
Shared Feature Ratio may not fully reflect the complexity of high-dimensional feature spaces.
Did not assess the interpretability of individual features through case studies.
future_direction: Exploring improved dataset generation and training strategies that could completely outperform Web-based methods.
Evaluating whether Faithful SAEs provide meaningful and interpretable explanations for individual features through detailed case studies.
Investigating the connection between pruning Fake Features and the principle of Minimal Description Length.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising solution for decomposing large language model representations into interpretable features. However, Paulo and Belrose (2025) have highlighted instability across different initialization seeds, and Heap et al. (2025) have pointed out that SAEs may not capture model-internal features. These problems likely stem from training SAEs on external datasets - either collected from the Web or generated by another model - which may contain out-of-distribution (OOD) data beyond the model's generalisation capabilities. This can result in hallucinated SAE features, which we term "Fake Features", that misrepresent the model's internal activations. To address these issues, we propose FaithfulSAE, a method that trains SAEs on the model's own synthetic dataset. Using FaithfulSAEs, we demonstrate that training SAEs on less-OOD instruction datasets results in SAEs being more stable across seeds. Notably, FaithfulSAEs outperform SAEs trained on web-based datasets in the SAE probing task and exhibit a lower Fake Feature Ratio in 5 out of 7 models. Overall, our approach eliminates the dependency on external datasets, advancing interpretability by better capturing model-internal features while highlighting the often neglected importance of SAE training datasets.

papers.title: Evaluating Adversarial Robustness of Concept Representations in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What is the robustness of concept representations in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to adversarial input perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces robustness as a critical evaluation dimension for sparse autoencoders (SAEs) and demonstrates that SAE concept representations are vulnerable to adversarial input perturbations.
papers.conclusion: SAE interpretations are highly vulnerable to minimal input changes, raising concerns about their reliability in realistic settings, and motivating the development of more robust interpretability tools.
papers.key_findings:
Small adversarial input perturbations can effectively manipulate SAE concept representations without notably affecting the base LLM's activations.
SAE concept representations are not robust even to non-adversarial synonym replacements.
The attacks are effective across different models, datasets, and model depths.
Untargeted attacks are more successful at the population level, while targeted attacks are more effective at the individual level.
SAE latents that represent meaningful concepts are highly manipulable.
papers.limitation:
The effectiveness of attacks is bounded by compute constraints (single 80GB A100 GPU).
The choice of medium-sized LLMs results in slower attacks.
future_direction: Developing novel methods to denoise SAE activations and isolate reliable signals.
Extending the evaluation framework to other concept-extraction tools like transcoders and crosscoders.
Optimizing the attack pipeline to better balance effectiveness and efficiency.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are commonly used to interpret the internal activations of large language models (LLMs) by mapping them to human-interpretable concept representations. While existing evaluations of SAEs focus on metrics such as the reconstruction-sparsity tradeoff, human (auto-)interpretability, and feature disentanglement, they overlook a critical aspect: the robustness of concept representations to input perturbations. We argue that robustness must be a fundamental consideration for concept representations, reflecting the fidelity of concept labeling. To this end, we formulate robustness quantification as input-space optimization problems and develop a comprehensive evaluation framework featuring realistic scenarios in which adversarial perturbations are crafted to manipulate SAE representations. Empirically, we find that tiny adversarial input perturbations can effectively manipulate concept-based interpretations in most scenarios without notably affecting the base LLM's activations. Overall, our results suggest that SAE concept representations are fragile and without further denoising or postprocessing they might be ill-suited for applications in model monitoring and oversight.

papers.title: Enhancing Neural Network Interpretability with Feature-Aligned Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the feature learning of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to better align with input features, thereby enhancing their usefulness for neural network interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Mutual Feature Regularization (MFR), a regularization technique that trains multiple Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) in parallel with weight reinitialization and an auxiliary penalty to encourage learning similar features, leading to better alignment with input features and improved SAE performance.
papers.conclusion: MFR encourages SAEs to learn more features of the input, thereby increasing their usefulness for neural network interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
MFR increases the correlation between feature similarity across SAEs and similarity with input features, as demonstrated on synthetic data.
On synthetic data, SAEs trained with MFR recover more of the known input features compared to baseline SAEs.
MFR improves reconstruction loss and loss recovered when training SAEs on GPT-2 Small MLP layer activations, with up to a 21.21% reduction in reconstruction loss.
MFR also improves reconstruction loss on EEG denoising tasks, though the benefits are smaller than for neural network activations.
The method involves conditionally reinitializing SAE weights based on inactive feature detection and adding an auxiliary penalty to encourage feature similarity across SAEs.
papers.limitation: MFR increases computational cost as it requires training multiple SAEs in parallel, which may become unmanageable for very large models.
future_direction: Investigate efficient mutual learning-based approaches for SAEs that can benefit from the positive relationship between feature similarity across SAEs and feature similarity with input features without requiring more compute.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promise in improving the interpretability of neural network activations, but can learn features that are not features of the input, limiting their effectiveness. We propose \textsc{Mutual Feature Regularization} \textbf{(MFR)}, a regularization technique for improving feature learning by encouraging SAEs trained in parallel to learn similar features. We motivate \textsc{MFR} by showing that features learned by multiple SAEs are more likely to correlate with features of the input. By training on synthetic data with known features of the input, we show that \textsc{MFR} can help SAEs learn those features, as we can directly compare the features learned by the SAE with the input features for the synthetic data. We then scale \textsc{MFR} to SAEs that are trained to denoise electroencephalography (EEG) data and SAEs that are trained to reconstruct GPT-2 Small activations. We show that \textsc{MFR} can improve the reconstruction loss of SAEs by up to 21.21\% on GPT-2 Small, and 6.67\% on EEG data. Our results suggest that the similarity between features learned by different SAEs can be leveraged to improve SAE training, thereby enhancing performance and the usefulness of SAEs for model interpretability.

papers.title: SAEs Are Good for Steering -- If You Select the Right Features
papers.research_question: How to distinguish between input and output features in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to improve the effectiveness of steering language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a taxonomy of SAE features into input and output types, introduces input and output scores to identify them, and demonstrates that selecting features with high output scores significantly improves steering performance, making unsupervised SAE steering competitive with supervised methods.
papers.conclusion: The work formalizes the roles of SAE features, provides practical scores for feature selection, and shows that output features are key to effective steering, bridging the gap between unsupervised and supervised steering methods.
papers.key_findings:
Features in SAEs can be categorized as input features, which capture input patterns, or output features, which influence model outputs.
High input and output scores rarely co-occur in the same features, with input features common in early layers and output features in later layers.
Features with high output scores are more effective for coherent and high-quality steering compared to those with high input scores.
Filtering SAE features based on output scores leads to 2-3x improvements in steering performance on benchmarks like AxBench.
With proper feature selection, SAE steering achieves performance close to supervised methods such as LoRA.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is restricted to features extracted from the residual stream, and does not account for features derived from other components such as attention or MLP layers.
Method focuses on steering using a single SAE feature, ignoring interactions between features that may lead to better effects.
future_direction: Understanding how multiple features combine or interfere for better steering effects.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have been proposed as an unsupervised approach to learn a decomposition of a model's latent space. This enables useful applications such as steering - influencing the output of a model towards a desired concept - without requiring labeled data. Current methods identify SAE features to steer by analyzing the input tokens that activate them. However, recent work has highlighted that activations alone do not fully describe the effect of a feature on the model's output. In this work, we draw a distinction between two types of features: input features, which mainly capture patterns in the model's input, and output features, which have a human-understandable effect on the model's output. We propose input and output scores to characterize and locate these types of features, and show that high values for both scores rarely co-occur in the same features. These findings have practical implications: after filtering out features with low output scores, we obtain 2-3x improvements when steering with SAEs, making them competitive with supervised methods.

papers.title: Measuring Sparse Autoencoder Feature Sensitivity
papers.research_question: How can we measure the sensitivity of Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features, i.e., how reliably they activate on texts similar to their activating examples?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a scalable, explanation-free method to evaluate SAE feature sensitivity, demonstrating that sensitivity is a novel dimension of feature quality and that many interpretable features have poor sensitivity, with sensitivity declining as SAE width increases.
papers.conclusion: The work establishes feature sensitivity as a crucial dimension for evaluating both individual SAE features and SAE architectures, emphasizing the need for better sensitivity in scaled SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Developed a generation-based method to evaluate SAE feature sensitivity without needing natural language descriptions.
Sensitivity measures a new aspect of feature quality, weakly correlated with existing metrics like interpretability and frequency.
Many interpretable SAE features have poor sensitivity, indicating they do not reliably activate on similar inputs.
Human evaluation confirms that generated text genuinely resembles activating examples when features fail to activate.
Average feature sensitivity declines with increasing SAE width across 7 SAE variants, highlighting a challenge in SAE scaling.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation limited to frequently occurring features, biasing analysis toward common features and missing rare features.
Filtering for features that remain active on truncated text may bias toward simpler features.
Does not incorporate activation magnitude into the sensitivity evaluation.
future_direction: Scale up evaluation to study less frequent features and use longer text snippets.
Incorporate activation strength into studies of SAE features.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features have become essential tools for mechanistic interpretability research. SAE features are typically characterized by examining their activating examples, which are often "monosemantic" and align with human interpretable concepts. However, these examples don't reveal feature sensitivity: how reliably a feature activates on texts similar to its activating examples. In this work, we develop a scalable method to evaluate feature sensitivity. Our approach avoids the need to generate natural language descriptions for features; instead we use language models to generate text with the same semantic properties as a feature's activating examples. We then test whether the feature activates on these generated texts. We demonstrate that sensitivity measures a new facet of feature quality and find that many interpretable features have poor sensitivity. Human evaluation confirms that when features fail to activate on our generated text, that text genuinely resembles the original activating examples. Lastly, we study feature sensitivity at the SAE level and observe that average feature sensitivity declines with increasing SAE width across 7 SAE variants. Our work establishes feature sensitivity as a new dimension for evaluating both individual features and SAE architectures.

papers.title: AbsTopK: Rethinking Sparse Autoencoders For Bidirectional Features
papers.research_question: Is the use of nonnegative activations truly essential for the success of SAEs, or does it constrain their ability to capture richer representations? Can SAEs be improved by allowing negative activations, enabling the discovery of bidirectional concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AbsTopK SAE, a sparse autoencoder variant that removes the non-negativity constraint, enabling single latent features to encode bidirectional semantic concepts and improving reconstruction fidelity and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Removing the non-negativity constraint in SAEs via the AbsTopK operator allows single features to capture bipolar semantics and yields reconstructions of superior compactness and fidelity, pioneering a shift towards bipolar sparse representations.
papers.key_findings:
AbsTopK SAE enables single latent features to encode opposing concepts by leveraging both positive and negative activations.
AbsTopK outperforms TopK and JumpReLU SAEs in reconstruction fidelity and interpretability across multiple models and tasks.
AbsTopK matches or even surpasses the supervised Difference-in-Mean method on some steering tasks.
The non-negativity constraint in existing SAEs fragments semantic axes into separate, redundant features, limiting representational completeness.
AbsTopK achieves a better balance between safety alignment (HarmBench) and general capability preservation (MMLU) compared to conventional SAE steering.
future_direction: Extending the framework to multi-step variants, yielding multi-layer encoders that produce more accurate sparse codes.
Investigating JumpReLU variants that apply a threshold on both positive and negative activations.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as powerful techniques for interpretability of large language models (LLMs), aiming to decompose hidden states into meaningful semantic features. While several SAE variants have been proposed, there remains no principled framework to derive SAEs from the original dictionary learning formulation. In this work, we introduce such a framework by unrolling the proximal gradient method for sparse coding. We show that a single-step update naturally recovers common SAE variants, including ReLU, JumpReLU, and TopK. Through this lens, we reveal a fundamental limitation of existing SAEs: their sparsity-inducing regularizers enforce non-negativity, preventing a single feature from representing bidirectional concepts (e.g., male vs. female). This structural constraint fragments semantic axes into separate, redundant features, limiting representational completeness. To address this issue, we propose AbsTopK SAE, a new variant derived from the $\ell_0$ sparsity constraint that applies hard thresholding over the largest-magnitude activations. By preserving both positive and negative activations, AbsTopK uncovers richer, bidirectional conceptual representations. Comprehensive experiments across four LLMs and seven probing and steering tasks show that AbsTopK improves reconstruction fidelity, enhances interpretability, and enables single features to encode contrasting concepts. Remarkably, AbsTopK matches or even surpasses the Difference-in-Mean method, a supervised approach that requires labeled data for each concept and has been shown in prior work to outperform SAEs.

papers.title: Position: Mechanistic Interpretability Should Prioritize Feature Consistency in SAEs
papers.research_question: How can feature consistency in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be achieved and measured to improve the reliability of mechanistic interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This position paper argues that mechanistic interpretability should prioritize feature consistency in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and proposes the Pairwise Dictionary Mean Correlation Coefficient (PW-MCC) as a practical metric to measure consistency. It shows that high consistency is achievable with appropriate architectural choices (e.g., TopK SAEs) and that high PW-MCC correlates with semantic similarity of feature explanations.
papers.conclusion: The paper calls for a community-wide shift towards valuing and systematically measuring feature consistency in SAEs for cumulative progress in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
High feature consistency (PW-MCC ≈ 0.80) is achievable with TopK SAEs on real-world LLM activations.
PW-MCC reliably tracks ground-truth feature recovery (GT-MCC) in synthetic experiments.
Feature consistency is frequency-dependent: more frequent features are learned more consistently.
Different SAE architectures yield different levels of consistency, with TopK SAEs performing best.
High PW-MCC scores correlate strongly with the semantic similarity of feature explanations.
papers.limitation:
The focus is on SAEs, and other interpretability methods may have different consistency challenges.
The study uses a specific metric (PW-MCC) for a specific notion of consistency (strong feature consistency).
The real-world experiments are limited to two base models and one dataset.
The automated interpretation pipeline has its own limitations.
future_direction: Extending consistency analysis to other interpretability methods beyond SAEs.
Developing more nuanced metrics for consistency that go beyond strong feature consistency.
Investigating the relationship between consistency and downstream task performance.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are a prominent tool in mechanistic interpretability (MI) for decomposing neural network activations into interpretable features. However, the aspiration to identify a canonical set of features is challenged by the observed inconsistency of learned SAE features across different training runs, undermining the reliability and efficiency of MI research. This position paper argues that mechanistic interpretability should prioritize feature consistency in SAEs -- the reliable convergence to equivalent feature sets across independent runs. We propose using the Pairwise Dictionary Mean Correlation Coefficient (PW-MCC) as a practical metric to operationalize consistency and demonstrate that high levels are achievable (0.80 for TopK SAEs on LLM activations) with appropriate architectural choices. Our contributions include detailing the benefits of prioritizing consistency; providing theoretical grounding and synthetic validation using a model organism, which verifies PW-MCC as a reliable proxy for ground-truth recovery; and extending these findings to real-world LLM data, where high feature consistency strongly correlates with the semantic similarity of learned feature explanations. We call for a community-wide shift towards systematically measuring feature consistency to foster robust cumulative progress in MI.

papers.title: Adaptive Sparse Allocation with Mutual Choice & Feature Choice Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be improved to allow adaptive computation and reduce dead features by variable allocation of sparsity budget per token and per feature?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Feature Choice and Mutual Choice SAEs, which allow adaptive computation by variable allocation of sparsity budget, and aux_zipf_loss, reducing dead features and improving reconstruction.
papers.conclusion: Feature Choice and Mutual Choice SAEs are simple drop-in improvements that enable adaptive computation and reduce dead features, advancing sparse autoencoder training for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Feature Choice and Mutual Choice SAEs achieve better reconstruction loss at equivalent sparsity levels compared to TopK SAEs.
Feature Choice SAEs result in zero dead features even at large scale, without complex resampling.
The aux_zipf_loss mitigates underutilized features and helps utilize SAE capacity more fully.
Feature densities in SAEs tend to follow a Zipf distribution, and constraining with Zipf distribution outperforms uniform distribution.
Adaptive computation allows difficult tokens to use more features and easy tokens to use fewer.
papers.limitation:
Appeals to the Monotonic Importance Heuristic may miss important low-magnitude activations.
Generalisation across modalities (e.g., audio, images) is untested.
Lack of widely agreed upon metrics for evaluating sparse autoencoders.
future_direction: Scaling laws for Feature Choice SAE performance on larger models.
Dissecting phenomenology of features conditioning on prevalence and activation magnitude.
Applying similar techniques to interpretability problems in other modalities.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a promising approach to extracting features from neural networks, enabling model interpretability as well as causal interventions on model internals. SAEs generate sparse feature representations using a sparsifying activation function that implicitly defines a set of token-feature matches. We frame the token-feature matching as a resource allocation problem constrained by a total sparsity upper bound. For example, TopK SAEs solve this allocation problem with the additional constraint that each token matches with at most $k$ features. In TopK SAEs, the $k$ active features per token constraint is the same across tokens, despite some tokens being more difficult to reconstruct than others. To address this limitation, we propose two novel SAE variants, Feature Choice SAEs and Mutual Choice SAEs, which each allow for a variable number of active features per token. Feature Choice SAEs solve the sparsity allocation problem under the additional constraint that each feature matches with at most $m$ tokens. Mutual Choice SAEs solve the unrestricted allocation problem where the total sparsity budget can be allocated freely between tokens and features. Additionally, we introduce a new auxiliary loss function, $\mathtt{aux\_zipf\_loss}$, which generalises the $\mathtt{aux\_k\_loss}$ to mitigate dead and underutilised features. Our methods result in SAEs with fewer dead features and improved reconstruction loss at equivalent sparsity levels as a result of the inherent adaptive computation. More accurate and scalable feature extraction methods provide a path towards better understanding and more precise control of foundation models.

papers.title: Modelling Cellular Perturbations with the Sparse Additive Mechanism Shift Variational Autoencoder
papers.research_question: How to model the effects of diverse interventions on cells to characterize unknown biological mechanisms of action, combining compositionality, disentanglement, and interpretability for perturbation models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SAMS-VAE, a generative model that combines sparsity, compositionality, and disentanglement for perturbation modeling, demonstrating improved predictive performance and interpretability on single-cell sequencing data.
papers.conclusion: SAMS-VAE is a useful model for perturbational screening data, with improved predictive performance and ability to recover factors correlated with biological mechanisms, and may aid in scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
SAMS-VAE with correlated inference achieves the best test IWELBO and average treatment effect correlation.
SAMS-VAE's latent mask is more predictive of annotated biological pathways than SVAE+.
SAMS-VAE and CPA-VAE perform well on out-of-distribution combinatorial tasks and in low-data settings.
SAMS-VAE improves prediction of nonlinear genetic interactions over a naive linear model.
Correlated inference strategies (correlated zbasal and correlated E) improve model performance.
papers.limitation: The prior on the mask may not enforce sparsity as desired when sample size increases, requiring adjustment of the prior strength to achieve desired sparsity.
future_direction: Studying how perturbations interact and compose in more complex fashion.
Incorporating different forms of prior knowledge into such systems.
papers.abstract: Generative models of observations under interventions have been a vibrant topic of interest across machine learning and the sciences in recent years. For example, in drug discovery, there is a need to model the effects of diverse interventions on cells in order to characterize unknown biological mechanisms of action. We propose the Sparse Additive Mechanism Shift Variational Autoencoder, SAMS-VAE, to combine compositionality, disentanglement, and interpretability for perturbation models. SAMS-VAE models the latent state of a perturbed sample as the sum of a local latent variable capturing sample-specific variation and sparse global variables of latent intervention effects. Crucially, SAMS-VAE sparsifies these global latent variables for individual perturbations to identify disentangled, perturbation-specific latent subspaces that are flexibly composable. We evaluate SAMS-VAE both quantitatively and qualitatively on a range of tasks using two popular single cell sequencing datasets. In order to measure perturbation-specific model-properties, we also introduce a framework for evaluation of perturbation models based on average treatment effects with links to posterior predictive checks. SAMS-VAE outperforms comparable models in terms of generalization across in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks, including a combinatorial reasoning task under resource paucity, and yields interpretable latent structures which correlate strongly to known biological mechanisms. Our results suggest SAMS-VAE is an interesting addition to the modeling toolkit for machine learning-driven scientific discovery.

papers.title: Interpreting Large Text-to-Image Diffusion Models with Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can sparse dictionary learning methods (Sparse Autoencoders and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations) be scaled and applied to interpret and control large text-to-image diffusion models?
papers.core_contribution: This work successfully scales Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations (ITDA) to a large text-to-image diffusion model (FLUX.1), demonstrating they can decompose residual stream activations into interpretable features and enable targeted steering of image generation.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Autoencoders and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations are effective methods for interpreting and steering large text-to-image diffusion models, with SAE features being particularly suitable for manipulating concrete semantic concepts in generated images.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs accurately reconstruct residual stream embeddings and outperform MLP neurons on automated interpretability metrics.
ITDA achieves comparable interpretability to SAEs but tends to encode more abstract visual attributes (colors, textures) while SAE features capture more concrete objects.
Steering image generation via SAE feature activation addition is effective but constrained, requiring the initial prompt to be semantically related to the steered feature.
The residual stream activations in FLUX.1 are highly anisotropic, necessitating PCA whitening for effective SAE training to avoid a high proportion of dead features.
ITDA generally achieves superior reconstruction performance compared to SAEs at similar dictionary sizes.
papers.limitation:
Automated interpretability (autointerp) metrics do not distinguish between abstract visual properties and manipulable semantic concepts, a qualitative difference observed between ITDA and SAE features.
Steering with SAE features is constrained and only effective when the initial image prompt is semantically related to the feature being added.
The autointerp pipeline may have biases, such as picking up on simple image characteristics like color rather than the intended semantic feature.
future_direction: Applying SAEs to vision tasks like classification, segmentation, and depth estimation (sparse probing).
Adapting the SAE encoder architecture to incorporate spatial inductive bias (e.g., convolutional layers) for image data.
Improving steering techniques, potentially by making the process more similar to finetuning or otherwise more aware of steering effects.
Investigating shared features between the text and image streams of the multimodal DiT architecture.
Comparing the two FLUX.1 variants (Dev and Schnell) using methods like crosscoders to find corresponding or unique features.
Investigating biases specific to the automated interpretability pipeline.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders are a promising new approach for decomposing language model activations for interpretation and control. They have been applied successfully to vision transformer image encoders and to small-scale diffusion models. Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations (ITDA) is a recently proposed variant of dictionary learning that takes the dictionary to be a set of data points from the activation distribution and reconstructs them with gradient pursuit. We apply Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and ITDA to a large text-to-image diffusion model, Flux 1, and consider the interpretability of embeddings of both by introducing a visual automated interpretation pipeline. We find that SAEs accurately reconstruct residual stream embeddings and beat MLP neurons on interpretability. We are able to use SAE features to steer image generation through activation addition. We find that ITDA has comparable interpretability to SAEs.

papers.title: Learning Multi-Level Features with Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we train sparse autoencoders to learn hierarchical features and avoid pathologies like feature absorption and splitting when scaling dictionary size?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders, a hierarchical variant that trains multiple nested dictionaries simultaneously to learn features at different levels of abstraction, reducing feature absorption and splitting.
papers.conclusion: Matryoshka SAEs are a superior alternative for practical interpretability tasks, enabling training of arbitrarily large SAEs while retaining interpretable features at different levels of abstraction.
papers.key_findings:
Matryoshka SAEs significantly reduce feature absorption and splitting compared to standard SAEs.
Matryoshka SAEs achieve more disentangled latent representations and better performance on sparse probing and targeted concept erasure tasks.
Matryoshka SAEs maintain or improve downstream task performance with increasing dictionary size, unlike standard SAEs which often degrade.
Matryoshka SAEs exhibit a small trade-off in reconstruction fidelity but learn more meaningful features that result in comparable downstream model loss.
The hierarchical structure forces early latents to capture general concepts and later latents to specialize, preserving interpretable features at multiple scales.
papers.limitation:
Slightly reduced reconstruction performance compared to standard SAEs.
Increased training time due to multiple nested reconstruction objectives.
Reliance on quantitative metrics that may not fully capture human-relevant interpretability.
future_direction: Investigate the human interpretability of Matryoshka SAE latents.
Explore the applicability of Matryoshka SAEs to practical interpretability tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful tool for interpreting neural networks by extracting the concepts represented in their activations. However, choosing the size of the SAE dictionary (i.e. number of learned concepts) creates a tension: as dictionary size increases to capture more relevant concepts, sparsity incentivizes features to be split or absorbed into more specific features, leaving high-level features missing or warped. We introduce Matryoshka SAEs, a novel variant that addresses these issues by simultaneously training multiple nested dictionaries of increasing size, forcing the smaller dictionaries to independently reconstruct the inputs without using the larger dictionaries. This organizes features hierarchically - the smaller dictionaries learn general concepts, while the larger dictionaries learn more specific concepts, without incentive to absorb the high-level features. We train Matryoshka SAEs on Gemma-2-2B and TinyStories and find superior performance on sparse probing and targeted concept erasure tasks, more disentangled concept representations, and reduced feature absorption. While there is a minor tradeoff with reconstruction performance, we believe Matryoshka SAEs are a superior alternative for practical tasks, as they enable training arbitrarily large SAEs while retaining interpretable features at different levels of abstraction.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Learn Monosemantic Features in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be applied to Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to improve interpretability and steerability, and how can we quantitatively evaluate the monosemanticity of neurons in such models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the MonoSemanticity score (MS) to evaluate neuron-level monosemanticity in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), validates MS with a human study, and demonstrates that SAEs can steer multimodal LLM outputs by intervening on vision encoder neurons.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) effectively improve neuron-level monosemanticity in Vision-Language Models, with the MonoSemanticity score providing a reliable metric aligned with human judgment, and shows that SAEs enable unsupervised concept-based steering of multimodal LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs significantly increase the monosemanticity of individual neurons in VLMs compared to original neurons.
Sparsity and wider latent dimensions are the most influential factors for improving monosemanticity.
Matryoshka SAEs achieve overall superior monosemanticity scores compared to standard SAE variants.
SAE interventions on the vision encoder can steer multimodal LLM (e.g., LLaVA) outputs to insert or suppress specific concepts without modifying the language model.
The proposed MonoSemanticity score aligns well with human perception of similarity, as validated by a large-scale user study.
papers.limitation:
High MS score neurons do not always produce precise effects when used to steer MLLM outputs; for example, a 'golden retriever' neuron might trigger any dog-related output due to limited fine-grained understanding in MLLMs.
A fraction of SAE neurons that act as feature detectors do not exhibit any clear steering effect.
future_direction: Adapting the MonoSemanticity metric to text representations.
Investigating the interplay between specialized (low-level) and broad (high-level) concepts within learned representations.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently gained attention as a means to improve the interpretability and steerability of Large Language Models (LLMs), both of which are essential for AI safety. In this work, we extend the application of SAEs to Vision-Language Models (VLMs), such as CLIP, and introduce a comprehensive framework for evaluating monosemanticity at the neuron-level in visual representations. To ensure that our evaluation aligns with human perception, we propose a benchmark derived from a large-scale user study. Our experimental results reveal that SAEs trained on VLMs significantly enhance the monosemanticity of individual neurons, with sparsity and wide latents being the most influential factors. Further, we demonstrate that applying SAE interventions on CLIP's vision encoder directly steers multimodal LLM outputs (e.g., LLaVA), without any modifications to the underlying language model. These findings emphasize the practicality and efficacy of SAEs as an unsupervised tool for enhancing both interpretability and control of VLMs. Code and benchmark data are available at https://github.com/ExplainableML/sae-for-vlm.

papers.title: Feature Hedging: Correlated Features Break Narrow Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Why do sparse autoencoders (SAEs) underperform relative to other techniques, and can we fix the problems? Specifically, the paper investigates the problem of 'feature hedging' in narrow SAEs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies 'feature hedging' as a fundamental problem in narrow sparse autoencoders (SAEs) where correlated features are merged, degrading monosemanticity, and proposes an improved variant called balance matryoshka SAEs to mitigate this issue.
papers.conclusion: Feature hedging is a core theoretical problem in SAEs that contributes to their underperformance, and the proposed balance matryoshka SAE architecture is a step towards addressing both hedging and absorption, though both problems remain.
papers.key_findings:
Feature hedging occurs when an SAE is too narrow to represent all underlying features and features are correlated, causing the SAE to merge components of correlated features into single latents.
Hedging is caused by the reconstruction (MSE) loss and becomes more severe the narrower the SAE.
In LLM SAEs, hedging is likely the norm due to the high number of correlated features and the SAE being narrower than the number of underlying features.
Balance matryoshka SAEs, which tune the relative loss coefficients between inner and outer levels, can improve performance by better balancing the competing forces of hedging and absorption.
SAE width is not a neutral hyperparameter: narrower SAEs suffer more from hedging, while wider SAEs suffer more from absorption.
papers.limitation: Only test hedging in SAEs up to 65k latents on LLMs with 2b parameters due to compute constraints.
future_direction: Improving balance matryoshka SAEs by learning different balancing coefficients per latent rather than a single coefficient for all latents.
papers.abstract: It is assumed that sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose polysemantic activations into interpretable linear directions, as long as the activations are composed of sparse linear combinations of underlying features. However, we find that if an SAE is more narrow than the number of underlying "true features" on which it is trained, and there is correlation between features, the SAE will merge components of correlated features together, thus destroying monosemanticity. In LLM SAEs, these two conditions are almost certainly true. This phenomenon, which we call feature hedging, is caused by SAE reconstruction loss, and is more severe the narrower the SAE. In this work, we introduce the problem of feature hedging and study it both theoretically in toy models and empirically in SAEs trained on LLMs. We suspect that feature hedging may be one of the core reasons that SAEs consistently underperform supervised baselines. Finally, we use our understanding of feature hedging to propose an improved variant of matryoshka SAEs. Importantly, our work shows that SAE width is not a neutral hyperparameter: narrower SAEs suffer more from hedging than wider SAEs.

papers.title: The Missing Curve Detectors of InceptionV1: Applying Sparse Autoencoders to InceptionV1 Early Vision
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders uncover interpretable features and address polysemantic neurons in InceptionV1's early vision layers?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable features from InceptionV1, revealing missing curve detectors and decomposing polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic features.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are a valuable tool for understanding InceptionV1 and convolutional neural networks, extending their promise beyond language models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs learn new interpretable features that were not visible when examining individual neurons.
SAEs discover additional curve detector features that fill gaps in the known family of curve detectors.
SAEs can split polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic constituent features.
papers.limitation: This paper is a very early report and does not defend the results in a systematic way.
future_direction: Investigate branch specialization and cross-branch superposition in InceptionV1 using SAEs.
papers.abstract: Recent work on sparse autoencoders (SAEs) has shown promise in extracting interpretable features from neural networks and addressing challenges with polysemantic neurons caused by superposition. In this paper, we apply SAEs to the early vision layers of InceptionV1, a well-studied convolutional neural network, with a focus on curve detectors. Our results demonstrate that SAEs can uncover new interpretable features not apparent from examining individual neurons, including additional curve detectors that fill in previous gaps. We also find that SAEs can decompose some polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic constituent features. These findings suggest SAEs are a valuable tool for understanding InceptionV1, and convolutional neural networks more generally.

papers.title: SOSAE: Self-Organizing Sparse AutoEncoder
papers.research_question: How can the dimensionality of an autoencoder's feature space be dynamically and optimally adapted without extensive hyperparameter tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SOSAE, a self-organizing sparse autoencoder that uses a novel push regularization to dynamically optimize the size of feature representations during training, achieving efficient compression and feature extraction.
papers.conclusion: SOSAE effectively optimizes feature representation size via push regularization, significantly reducing computational and memory costs while maintaining model performance across various image datasets.
papers.key_findings:
SOSAE compresses input into significantly smaller feature lengths (3.1 to 4.3 times more compression) than baseline autoencoders while maintaining or improving classification accuracy.
SOSAE reduces FLOPs usage by 23.3% to 32% and memory usage significantly compared to baselines, due to structured sparsity and truncation of non-active neurons.
The feature vectors generated by SOSAE are robust to truncation; removing trailing dimensions does not cause information loss, unlike other sparse autoencoder variants.
SOSAE achieves optimal hidden layer dimensionality with up to 130 times fewer FLOPs than grid search and 34 times fewer than random search for hyperparameter tuning.
SOSAE demonstrates better denoising performance and robustness against zero-masking and Gaussian noise compared to Denoising Autoencoders, while using shorter feature representations.
papers.abstract: The process of tuning the size of the hidden layers for autoencoders has the benefit of providing optimally compressed representations for the input data. However, such hyper-parameter tuning process would take a lot of computation and time effort with grid search as the default option. In this paper, we introduce the Self-Organization Regularization for Autoencoders that dynamically adapts the dimensionality of the feature space to the optimal size. Inspired by physics concepts, Self-Organizing Sparse AutoEncoder (SOSAE) induces sparsity in feature space in a structured way that permits the truncation of the non-active part of the feature vector without any loss of information. This is done by penalizing the autoencoder based on the magnitude and the positional index of the feature vector dimensions, which during training constricts the feature space in both terms. Extensive experiments on various datasets show that our SOSAE can tune the feature space dimensionality up to 130 times lesser Floating-point Operations (FLOPs) than other baselines while maintaining the same quality of tuning and performance.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Reveal Temporal Difference Learning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models implement temporal difference learning to solve reinforcement learning problems in-context, despite being trained only for next-token prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models implement temporal difference learning for in-context reinforcement learning, and sparse autoencoders can reveal and causally manipulate these representations.
papers.conclusion: The work shows that large language models implement temporal difference learning for in-context reinforcement learning, and sparse autoencoders provide a methodology for studying and manipulating these mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Llama 3 70B can solve simple reinforcement learning problems in-context and its behavior is best described by a Q-learning model.
Sparse autoencoders trained on the residual stream reveal features that correlate with temporal difference errors and Q-values.
